speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON RESIGNATION OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I returned from London on Saturday morning I have given careful consideration, with my colleagues, to the situation which arose in the house on Friday, June 29 and on Monday, July 2.
I have also, as I am sure every hon. member would have expected me to do, seen Mr. Speaker and discussed the situation with him.
I think all of us can understand the desire of the Speaker to be able to answer fully and freely the criticisms levelled against him as a result of the position in which he had been placed by members of two of the opposition parties who supported the motion which was moved on June 4, and which asked this house to say that it no longer had any confidence in its presiding officer.
It is not hard to understand the reactions of any man, regardless of the office he may occupy, who feels he has been unfairly charged and has not, himself, been able to reply to those charges.
I am sure most hon. members will sympathize with the desire of the Speaker to place himself, as soon as possible, on a basis of equality with other hon. members so he will have freedom to explain the conduct, which was vindicated by the very large majority which rejected the motion I have just referred to.
And that, I understand, is the position Mr. Speaker wished to achieve when he stated on Monday of last week that he was placing his resignation before the house to take effect at the pleasure of the house.
Of course, all hon. members are aware that such a statement or declaration of intention does not constitute the formal action required as the actual resignation of a Speaker.
Because of my absence in London, Mr. Speaker refrained from taking any such formal action so that I might have the
opportunity to consider the situation, and for that I wish to thank him.
As Prime Minister I have the ultimate responsibility for the leadership of the house, and I do not intend to shirk that responsibility in any way.
I have had to ask myself whether the matter referred to by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and others on Friday, June 29, really has sufficient gravity to justify the resignation of a Speaker who recently received an overwhelming vote of confidence from the house.
I have no hesitation in saying I do not think so.
I share, and I am sure most hon. members share, the regret of the Speaker that any part of his personal letter was published. I cannot, however, share the view that because the Speaker had expressed in private the views he did express in that letter, he could no longer continue to be an impartial and competent Speaker. It does not seem to me that the publication by someone else of an extract from a private letter would justify me, or the majority in this house, in taking any formal action in consequence of what has taken place.
During the debate on the motion relating to his conduct and subsequently Mr. Speaker has discharged his duties in this house with dignity and impartiality.
My confidence in Mr. Speaker is unshaken, and I know of no other member better qualified than he is to preside over our deliberations; I believe that confidence is shared by an overwhelming majority of members, a majority by no means confined to the supporters of the government.
Now, as the one responsible for the leadership in this house, 1 have expressed that view to Mr. Speaker and I have found that he was willing to subordinate his personal feelings to his duty to parliament and the country, and to continue in the office in which he has served with great distinction. I am happy to be able to make that announcement to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement now on the matters discussed at the conference, which can be taken into account by hon. members who wish to discuss this subject upon the estimates of the Department of External Affairs which it is planned to discuss soon.
The statement of the conference-which, as always, represented a lot of work in achieving points of substance and forms of expression to which all could agree-indicates that the main subjects of discussion were in the field of international affairs. Problems of the commonwealth, as such, did not require very much attention. It is functioning as we expect it to function and adapting itself to changing conditions. It is primarily an association of nations having a common heritage of British parliamentary institutions, and many elements of common purpose in their approach to the problems of the day, despite the great differences in the geography, history and cultures of the various constituent nations.
The purpose for which we meet is the important and constructive one of exchanging information and opinions, in the hope that thereby the governments and parliaments of member countries can and will make wiser decisions. The conference does not seek to take any collective decisions or actions itself, but hopes to assist in bringing points of view closer together.
The commonwealth of today has not been the product of any political theory. It has developed from the practical response of sensible men to the desire for a continuing and close political relationship which adds to rather than detracts from the independence of its members. For most member countries, a common allegiance to the same crown is a link between us which we hold very dear. For the other, republican members, the Queen is none the less the head of the commonwealth. In discussion around the table, there is no distinction between members, and all prime ministers joined in frankly and fully setting their views in confidence before their colleagues, and in questioning one another.
I should like to lay special emphasis upon the value I find in having the prime ministers of the Asian members of the commonwealth at our conference table. The histories and cultures, the peoples and problems of these nations, are so different from our own that if is of great value in dealing with major international affairs to have the benefit of discussions with their leaders.
The development of Asian nationalism is one of the great historic movements of our time. Indeed, in some ways it is more comprehensive and significant than the rise of

militant communism. The wise counsel of the outstanding commonwealth Asian leaders of this great movement is something I find most helpful in trying to understand the perplexities of this complicated world in which we must now accept our share of responsibilities.
The London communique indicates the main subjects we discussed. They include our relations with Soviet Russia, the problem of security and stability in Europe, the current situation in the Middle East, the developments in southeast Asia, our relations with China, the economic position of the countries in the sterling area and the development of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes. In addition, there were many private talks on a variety of subjects, and those members of the commonwealth who are linked by special defence agreements, such as NATO, met to consider certain aspects of defence policy.
I cannot, of course, give a detailed account of the discussions which were held in confidence and on which we issued this agreed statement. I should like to take a minute or two, however, to say a little from my own point of view about several of the matters we discussed.
First, on relations with Soviet Russia, the communique makes clear that we all felt that the changes that have been taking place in the Soviet government, and its attitudes and policies, may have more than merely a feigned or superficial significance. Events will tell. This situation offers opportunities for improvement in our relations with Russia and perhaps opportunities for the settlement of outstanding difficulties between Russia and the western nations. All commonwealth governments plan to seek and use such opportunities and will welcome any improvement in relations with Russia which they may make possible. But the changes that have taken place are not such that we can have confidence that the danger of war has been removed. In view of this and of the tremendous Russian military power, and the evidence we have had in the past of the possibility of aggressive intentions, I believe we must continue to maintain an effective modern armed strength, primarily of course as a deterrent against attack. Such preparedness, however, need not prejudice an improvement in our relations and the development of a greater degree of mutual confidence which would be a more secure foundation for a lasting peace.
In the discussions on China we exchanged views, of course, on the recognition of the government on the mainland. While the views of most of us are already fairly well known,
I found the discussions both informative and
Commonwealth Conference helpful. I recognize the force of the arguments about the importance to Asia of having its largest country fully participating in the councils of the world. To that view, of course, we must give great weight and we shall. But there are other considerations as well which must weigh in determining Canada's policy and course of action. I see no reason strong enough to justify changing our policy on this matter at this time.
Our discussions in regard to the Middle East naturally centred on the danger of conflict between the Arab states and Israel. On the whole I was somewhat reassured by what I heard. We all recognize that the situation there is dangerous, but the danger has become a little less acute as a result of Mr. Hammarskjold's mediation. I feel that every effort should be made now through the security council of the United Nations to secure the collaboration of the Soviet union in helping to find a peaceful settlement of this Palestine issue. I think they realize the danger there would be to them as well as to the rest of the world from war breaking out in that area.
Our discussions of economic affairs were in the nature of interim reports and analyses of the situation in the sterling area members of the commonwealth. They were naturally of very considerable interest to us, for the situation of all these countries, particularly of Britain, affects our trade. I gave a brief resume of some aspects of our situation likely to be of interest to others. The United Kingdom government is persevering in its efforts to find solutions to its own economic problems that would permit an increasing freedom of trade between us and the continued elimination of discrimination against imports from the dollar area. We recognized and valued the progress made already in this direction and naturally we expressed the wish to see this progress continue. We were assured that the United Kingdom intended to persevere with this policy and I think the events and public statements in the United Kingdom in recent weeks make this determination quite evident. I am convinced that our policy should continue to be to seek the removal of the remaining restrictions on the imports of Canadian goods into the United Kingdom and elsewhere in the sterling area and to encourage the development of sound competitive export trade from the United Kingdom to Canada.
This trade remains under the detailed scrutiny of our continuing joint committee of senior officers which was established for that purpose and which met in London earlier in June.

There was no discussion at this conference about the time or place of our next meeting.
I have been asked whether a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers might be held in Canada and to this I would reply that we should be glad and honoured to have a future meeting here but the time and place of any particular meeting must be determined primarily by the convenience of the busy men who are required to attend. London has proved to be a convenient site but this does not mean that the conference should not be held in other commonwealth capitals when that is the general desire.
I should like to take advantage of this jpportunity to express again the gratitude jf all the Canadians attending this conference for the hospitality and friendliness with which we were received by Her Majesty ;he Queen and by all those in the United Kingdom who joined in making the conference a success.

speechtext:
I might make a short statement in reply to those questions and the point raised by my friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I am sure that all hon. members of this house condemn certain methods which the Polish authorities have seen fit to use in suppressing the decent peaceful demonstrations of the people of Poznan, Poland, who have asked only for bread and freedom from their communist rulers. These methods of the police state are deserving of the strongest censure on the part of all nations and peoples who respect human liberty and dignity; all the more so because of the recent talks about "liberalization" and "democratization" in Poland. If the Polish government wish us to believe that there is any reality behind their use of these words, they will apply these principles to the people of Poznan, especially in regard to action taken against those who have been arrested and who are entitled to a justice which excludes, in the words of the hon. member for Prince Albert, "cruel and unnatural punishment".
It is a telling commentary on what communists call a "worker's paradise" that, in the midst of an international fair designed to demonstrate to the world the material progress of Poland since the war, the workers

should be driven by hunger and despair to demonstrate against food shortages and against the oppression of the regime. In spite of the steps being taken against the people of Poznan, and, in fact, because of my deep sympathy and great admiration for them -which is, of course, shared by all members of the house-it would, I am afraid, be useless and perhaps unwise to direct an official request to the Polish government as to how they should handle the situation. Such an official request would be taken by that government simply as unwarranted interference in their internal affairs, and the reaction in Warsaw might be directed against the people of Poznan themselves, whom we would be trying to help.
I am sure that no one in this house, and especially none of the people of Polish descent in Canada who are so rightly aroused by these events in their motherland, would want the Canadian government to take any action which might bring further suffering upon their compatriots in Poland who have shown us that the Polish tradition of courage and the Polish passion for freedom are still strong and vital. I can assure the house that I would have no hesitation in recommending such action if I thought it had any chance of achieving our principal aim, which is the alleviation of the lot of the people concerned.
We can, however, do this. We can make clear our condemnation of any cruel and police-state methods of repression used or contemplated by the Polish communist authorities. We can express our fervent hope that these authorities may learn that the ancient yearning of the people of Poland for freedom and a better material life cannot be indefinitely suppressed by force. Finally-and I assure the house that we will do this-we can see that this statement of our views is brought to the attention of the Polish government.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been reminded today in some of the statements that have been made that we are living through a period of dramatic change which affects us and every other nation. It is my intention in the remarks that I shall make to discuss Canada and our own future in the changing scene.
The whole of Europe has marched ahead since the end of the last world war in a way that no one would have dreamed possible during the grim days of war itself. Not only have nations which were crushed under the impact of war found a new vitality and a new strength but nations which had not previously existed have taken form. New nations have emerged in Asia, Africa and elsewhere which will have a profound effect upon the course of our own life in the years ahead. Nowhere have those changes been more remarkable than within the commonwealth. Today we have had a brief report from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) about the conference which has recently taken place in London. Following that conference a statement was issued which placed a very optimistic interpretation upon the meeting itself. I think it will be the hope of all of us that the optimistic expectations will be fulfilled. I must confess that we have little information before us now as to what the details are which justify those expectations. We regret very deeply that the government of Canada did not extend an invitation for a trade and economic conference here in Ottawa to be attended by the prime ministers of all the governments of the commonwealth. After all, the beginning of any meeting of that kind rests upon a positive invitation.
We have been stressing for years our belief that it is in the interests of Canada as well as the other parts of the commonwealth that every possible step be taken to vitalize the exchange of goods and to bring into as close harmony as possible those nations which are associated in this amazing fellowship. I would hope that the day is not too far distant when it will be possible for such an invitation to be extended in a manner that will leave no uncertainty that we in Canada desire the very fullest possible co-operation in every way with the United Kingdom and other nations of the commonwealth.

As we look forward into the distant years ahead not one of us can see what may happen in that future period. Let us hope and pray that in the uncharted course that lies beyond the immediate future the commonwealth may emerge as the great central core of international understanding and that the unique fellowship which found expression in London in recent days may give confidence to others for international harmony and good will and find living expression without weakening national sovereignty in any way.
Behind every consideration of the future must be a recognition of the reality of the Soviet empire. By steps which need not now be recounted in detail Russia has established a terrible sovereignty over the colonial system which by one of the strangest ironies of history has emerged at the very time that, by the voluntary acts of other great powers, colonial systems elsewhere have been disappearing. Only recently we have seen something of what that authority means in the steps that have been taken in Poland to suppress the expression in that country of the desire for freedom. The reality of Russian domination of nearly one-third of the world's people and the reality of the attempts of Russia to affect our life in so many ways, both in our internal activities as well as otherwise, impresses upon us the need for examining our position and considering how best we can strengthen ourselves not only for the immediate present but for the long years which lie ahead.
What will historians one hundred years hence record of the events which will occur during the lives of ourselves, our children and our children's children? Will it be told that freedom was engulfed in an ever-widening flood of communist oppression, or will the story be a bright narrative of spreading freedom which saw its beginning in such events as those which occurred in the last few days in Poznan or other similar events which have happened elsewhere in East Germany and other places behind the iron curtain? Of one thing we can be sure. The course will be determined in large measure by the degree to which freedom itself is cherished and protected in the countries which are still free and in the degree of unity which is maintained among the nations sharing freedom at this time.
As we read the history of the events which preceded the beginning of the dark ages- and they are set forth with dramatic colour and vigour in the recent history published by Sir Winston Churchill-we are reminded that the advanced civilization of the early Christian era almost disappeared because of complacency and uncertainty about the value of united effort to stem the tide of aggression 67509-367
9, 1956	5773
Natural Resources-Development which on every frontier threatened the survival of a civilization which in arts and letters even if not in technical development had equalled or even surpassed our own civilization of today. Our own part in maintaining this priceless freedom will be measured not only in our material advancement and our contribution to the joint defence of freedom but also by the extent to which we speak as a free and sovereign nation capable in every way of making our own special contribution to the common cause and making that contribution as a result of decisions that are entirely our own.
If one lesson comes to us more clearly than any other from the long history of the past it is that our best contribution in the international field as well as in the field of domestic development will be to speak as Canadians on behalf of Canadians with visions of a strong and growing Canada always before us in our thoughts. We Canadians have hardly yet grasped the full significance of what has been happening since the end of the second world war. We have seen things happening around us which had their beginning in that war itself. Because of the unparalleled use of resources during the war and the need to repair the awful destruction of those terrible years, demands on new resources of raw material and resources generally have become far greater than ever before. On top of this have come remarkable scientific and technical discoveries in so many fields which were stimulated by the demands of war itself.
It is in such a situation and under such conditions that we find ourselves in possession of enormous resources of so many kinds. We have all the resources in this country to support a large, prosperous and happy population. We have the agricultural land; we have the forests; we have the fuel; we have the raw materials for buildings; we have all the things that are needed for a really great development here within our own boundaries. With all this we have practically every mineral needed in this mineral age. The only important metal for which we have not the raw material in Canada is aluminum; yet in that case because of our huge hydroelectric resources we are importing bauxite from Jamaica and British Guiana on a scale which ranks us as the world's second producer of this immensely valuable metal, and there is reason to believe that we will soon be the first. It is a fabulous picture of opportunity which opens out before the people of Canada today.
I am not going to go into all the statistics to support the statement that at this time

Natural Resources-Development Canadians have a greater opportunity for the future than any other people in the world. The facts are there; there is the reality. What a story of rewarding adventure it has already been. Just let us think, as we look into the future, of the new discoveries which within so small a number of years have changed the whole picture here in Canada and in some measure changed the picture throughout the world.
It is only about 25 years ago that Gilbert LaBine in that romantic flight of his in the sub-Arctic saw the first signs of uranium and by the discovery which came later started a new phase in Canada's mineral possibilities when the reality of those uranium deposits became known. Before that the existence of this mineral had been unknown in Canada. Now it seems that we shall soon be the world's largest producer with the discoveries which have recently been made.
The same story is being repeated in so many fields of development. Ten years ago we were relatively small producers of iron and the fabulous deposits in eastern Quebec and Labrador had still to be proved. Our oil production was still small; and up until a few years ago natural gas was being used only by those fortunate enough to live near the actual sources of supply. Just in those few passing years, from the Atlantic to the Pacific vast new deposits of iron ore have been discovered, oil production is mounting by leaps and bounds and spreading over a wider area all the time, and huge reserves of natural gas have been added to our fuel supplies. It is a truly fantastic picture.
Not only have we almost every mineral in the calendar from antimony to zinc, we have them in large commercial quantities, we have them in amounts that make it possible for us to contemplate the industrial use of every one of them. The question we must ask ourselves is, what is this going to mean to Canadians in the years ahead? We have everything to make this a great and populous industrial nation. We have the resources, we have the industrial power, we have the fuel-producing capacity and the basic requirements for housing, clothing and heat for a very large population. We can grow vast quantities of food. We grow enough wheat for 100 million people. We can expand our food production to support a very large population by intensive agricultural methods throughout the whole country.
What lies before us is much more than the opportunity for growth which is taking place in other parts of the world today. If only we perceive the full possibilities now opening up before us we will find, not that we are at the beginning of a period of steady

advance but that we are just now at the threshold of one of those historic upsurges in the life of a nation which have carried one country after another to positions of commanding importance throughout the centuries.
But this is not going to happen just for the reason alone that we happen to have natural resources. That is a fallacy which it would be well for us to keep in perspective. The way that these resources will be used will depend upon positive decisions. We cannot emphasize to ourselves too often the fact that resources alone do not bring power and lasting prosperity. There are far too many stories in the pages of history which tell us of the temporary wealth, sometimes great wealth, of nations which lived on their resources without any thought for the future and then sank into relative unimportance after those resources had been exhausted.
On the other hand, many nations have become strong and prosperous with practically no raw materials in their possession. They overcame their difficulties by industry, technical skill and a great national spirit. Of all the nations which offer an example of what can be done, the United Kingdom stands supreme. With relatively few natural resources as we know them, they became the great trading nation of the world in the last century simply by the energy, productive capacity and skill of the people of those famous islands.
Let us look at other examples. One small nation which tells us what can be done even without resources is Switzerland. It has practically no raw materials of any kind except its forests, its soil and its streams, but the application of research and great technical skill combined with industry and a national determination has made it one of the most prosperous countries in the world today.
When that can be done without resources, think of what can be done with the resources we possess if in this country of ours, the third largest in the world, we apply the same principles, the same spirit and the same policies to the tasks which lie before us.
We have much reason for satisfaction here in Canada. We have one of the highest material living standards in the world. But we have no reason for complacency. We are not manufacturing all that we could manufacture from our own raw materials. We are not processing nearly as much of our raw material as should be processed by Canadians here in Canada. The simple and inescapable fact is that, while we can point with a great measure of satisfaction to many areas of concentrated industrial development, we have not been keeping pace with

many other countries in industrial development during recent years, in spite of our tremendous opportunities.
Another thing which has a great bearing on our own future is the fact that the discovery of the full extent of our mineral and other resources has come at a time when the United States has in a very substantial measure exhausted many of their own. Because of our geographical position there is a tendency to seek from Canadian sources raw materials for a huge industrial production in the United States. It is to our immediate advantage to ship much of our raw material to the United States, just as it is to our immediate advantage to buy certain raw materials from them; but it is also to our immediate and urgent advantage that, while the development of these resources is being opened up and these resources are being shipped to the United States, we also take appropriate steps to make sure that here in Canada we are giving employment to Canadians at the highest level of wages by processing just as many of those resources as we possibly can.
The thing that we must remember and that we are inclined to forget is that no raw materials are inexhaustible. The United States thought their raw materials were beyond any level of exhaustion; then suddenly they came face to face a few years ago with the reality of their situation. In the Paley report, which was the report of a very competent commission set up to examine the situation in the United States, they were told to the amazement of many of them, that in the case of a great many of the resources the United States was going to be a have-not country within 25 years.
According to the latest figures of the dominion bureau of statistics, the only mineral in Canada which might seem to be comparatively inexhaustible is iron ore. Even in that case it would not be wise for us to assume that there is not some point of exhaustion, if we discuss these problems in terms of history and not of the immediate present. If we become the main supplier of a tremendously expanded steel industry in the United States throughout the years ahead, and if they should be in a position to determine what the main end product of those resources will be and how those resources will be used, then we might find ourselves in the position that even with our huge reserves they could in time, with their enormously expanded production, exhaust our own resources of iron just as they have their own. That, however, is the one case where we have any reason to use the term "inexhaustible resources", except in the case of forest products, where there is a renewable resource 67509-3674

Once a country is fully opened up, it is opened up for all time; with new technical devices and new means of transportation we are well on the way to the real opening up of our country. As trustees for future generations of Canadians, we should make sure in every way we can, within the framework of our constitutional structure, that by the combined efforts of all governments and all the people of Canada the opening up of our country brings the maximum benefit to every part of Canada, not only for today but for future generations far into the years ahead.
We see many signs of great increases in industrial production in Canada, but again it is well for us to temper our satisfaction with statistics. In spite of new sources of industrial energy and great new supplies of raw materials for industrial production, we have not kept pace with the rest of the free world in industrial expansion, as I have already mentioned. The United Nations monthly bulletin of statistics for January 1956 reports that the increase of industrial production for the whole non-communist world was 37 per cent between the years 1948 and 1954 inclusive, while for the same period Canada's industrial expansion was 24 per cent. In the same period the industrial production of West Germany expanded 180 per cent. I, of course,

speechtext: You mean, from the paralysis following the second world war?

speechtext:
I concede immediately that there are unusual circumstances that produced that result, and I was just going to say when the minister interrupted my remarks that these cannot be compared with our own figures, because Germany was rebuilding a great industrial structure after the destruction of the world war. Nevertheless, in the United Kingdom, where there also had been destruction, there has also been a greater percentage of industrial expansion than there has been in Canada. This is not something in regard to which we need to be unduly concerned, having regard to the future; it is simply, as I said before, something to temper our optimism and make us recognize that with the unique opportunities we possess, unequalled by any other country today of anything approaching a similar population, we have not done all that could be done in the way of industrial expansion.
There is also the fact that the improvement in personal income, which has been substantial, has not been equally distributed throughout our country. In terms of real dollar value there has been a surprisingly small increase in the maritime provinces and Saskatchewan, with some areas in the other provinces equally unbalanced. Large areas right across Canada have not participated fully in our recent growth and development. This government has failed to meet its obligations to those parts of Canada which are most in need of encouragement and financial support. The failure of this government to support sound projects like the South Saskatchewan power and irrigation project, the Beech wood project in New Brunswick and other similar developments which have been discussed here from time to time merely serve to accentuate the differences already existing not only in different parts of this country but in the way in which this government deals with the problems in different parts of the country.
The present government's policy for Canada's economic growth exposes this country to severe external dangers which could be reduced if greater encouragement were given to the building within Canada of heavy and light industry while at the same time increasing the size of our domestic market by well-planned immigration.
Our growth has been the result of a vigorous pioneering spirit over the long years amongst our own people combined with foreign investment in our development through the whole of our national history.

From Britain, France, Germany and now more particularly from the United States money has flowed into Canada because of the prospects offered for a sure return. That, after all, has been the inducement:	The
prospect of returns from the investment made.
We have always welcomed foreign investment and I am sure we always shall. But we should not exaggerate our dependence on foreign investment. More than 80 per cent of all capital investment in Canada still comes from Canadians. However, the important fact which we must examine and discuss from the point of view of government policy is the growing danger to our economy as a result of the ownership by residents of the United States of a very large proportion of Canadian industries and mineral production. The latest official figures available are those for 1952. According to those figures we are told that 38 per cent of the capital in Canadian manufacturing industry was owned in the United States, and 53 per cent in mining, smelting and the petroleum group of industries. That proportion has rapidly increased since those figures were made available. It has been estimated in the press recently that 90 per cent of our oil industry is controlled in the United States. It may not yet have reached that point. Certain it is, however, that the percentage of ownership in the vital industries which profoundly affect the course of our economic growth is rapidly increasing all the time. It is not enough to say that these industries and other producing activities must of necessity operate to the advantage of Canada because they are in Canada and under Canadian law. The fact is that this government has on different occasions answered people who have complained of certain difficulties that arise because of the foreign ownership of industry here, that they could not control the result of that ownership. Companies which are controlled in the United States, whether they be Canadian companies or United States companies, are controlled effectively outside Canada as to their plans of production, their pricing policies, their dividend policies and the policy of the company as to further extensions of their activities and the direction of their production. The laws of Canada do not affect their control over those fundamental and vital aspects of their activities. Already this represents a substantial loss of economic independence in many lines of production.
Our position is different from that of any other country in the world today. It is well for us to keep in mind the broad map of the world and the relationship of other countries throughout the world. Nowhere is there a situation similar to that with which

we are confronted. We live side by side with a great and friendly neighbour. No sinister purpose guides their attitude towards us. Over the years, right across Canada there has been a mingling of blood that extends family relationships with the people of the United States. Nevertheless, there is this unusual situation. We live side by side with a country which has a direct and daily impact upon our thinking through the press, over the radio, by television, through the periodical publications and by other means of communication. In this way the desire to buy things produced in the United States is stimulated in a manner that is perfectly legitimate for those who are selling and producing those products in the United States. Nevertheless, the reality is there. The steady pressure of financial expansion from the United States into Canada has created an interlocking economy in which the direction is swinging more and more to the head offices of companies in the United States which are operating on both sides of the border. It is as though there were two great bodies living side by side, with the arteries becoming more and more intertwined but the central control of those arteries moving more and more into the more populous of the two countries.
Let us examine these facts in the manner in which we are accustomed to examine them when we discuss situations of this kind with our friends in the United States. After all, it is to their interest as well as ours that Canada be a strong and vigorous nation, confident in its own right and in a position to build to the full stature of powerful nationhood under the control of our own policies in the years ahead. Here are some of the results of the situation which is developing:
1.	A heavy net outflow of interest and dividends increases the amount of goods which have to be shipped abroad to raise the necessary foreign exchange. In other words, the profits are drained out of the country and the amount of goods which can be imported at any given level proportionately reduced.
2.	Foreign interests control the pricing policies of their Canadian subsidiaries in a way that could be a great disadvantage to the Canadian consumer.
3.	Foreign financial control is in a position to decide the extent and the form of the operations of their Canadian subsidiaries, and they can use earnings from their Canadian subsidiaries to finance expansion of plants outside of Canada.
4.	In many cases senior positions in Canadian subsidiaries are held by other than Canadians.
Natural Resources-Development
5.	Foreign management may use its Canadian plant to manufacture goods for export only when the United States plant is too busy to handle its export orders. This creates undesirable fluctuations in production and employment in the Canadian subsidiary.
6.	A foreign-owned subsidiary can export scarce goods to the parent company's foreign consumers even if prices for the product are higher in Canada. That has already happened in cases that have been discussed.
7.	A foreign company may not give the Canadian public adequate information about the affairs of its Canadian subsidiary. A number of Canadian subsidiaries today are operating under laws which do not compel them to give the information which is essential for an understanding of their operation.
8.	United States interests doing business in Canada are subject to some laws of the United States such as the anti-trust laws. No matter how desirable the purpose of any of those laws may be, the result is that there can be an interference with business in Canada by the decision of the United States courts or other tribunals. I submit that business in Canada should be under Canadian courts and tribunals only.
9.	Industrial research for Canadian owned subsidiaries of foreign owned corporations may be carried on outside the country so that there may not be adequate inducement for skilled personnel to remain in Canada.
A number of these disadvantages could be met without in any way discouraging investment in Canada and with comparatively simple changes to Canadian laws. For example, there should be a Canadian law to compel the United States owners of substantial Canadian subsidiaries to publish properly audited balance sheets and income statements of their Canadian operations. If this were done the Canadian public would know how profitable those subsidiaries are and what the actual cost of production is in relation to price. Those are some of the obvious disadvantages that arise from a situation which has developed simply from the fact that Canada now offers a rich return for large scale investment.
We have gained a great deal from that investment. We all recognize that. We must recognize that we have also gained much from the association of Canadian business with large United States businesses, as we have from the association with British businesses, with French businesses, with German businesses and other businesses that have set up for operation here in Canada. We gained the advantage of their technical skill, their industrial experience and their elaborate
5778	HOUSE OF
Natural Resources-Development research facilities. On the other hand, carried to its ultimate conclusion, this could produce the result that we would not have adequate research facilities of our own; that we would not develop the necessary management skills and that our business methods, which in the end have such a wide impact upon our social conditions, would not be under our own direction.
Therefore, it seems clear that if we do believe it is important that we remain Canadians and have a distinct Canadian nationality, it is desirable that those steps be taken which are necessary to encourage our own management and expansion of our own affairs. This can be done without in any way discouraging legitimate investment of any kind in Canada. One of the most important things in industrial expansion is research. The amazingly successful industries of Switzerland and Holland, both tiny countries compared with the size of ours, are an example of what can be accomplished in that field. So also is the immense production of Germany and that, of course, is true of the United States. Therefore, the training of skilled men and women to take their part in research and technical development must be part of the national program consciously designed to advance our industrial expansion in Canada.
Without interfering in any way with the exclusive jurisdiction over education which rests with provincial governments, encouragement should be given to advance research and within the framework of our constitution research facilities should be expanded rapidly right across Canada in our universities and industries. This is something the government can do and should undertake right away.
This government has been strangely reluctant to make those changes in our laws which would end the very real discrimination against Canadian investors. It does seem a strange thing that a situation actually exists today that Canadian investors are in many respects at a disadvantage when it comes to investment in Canada as compared with investors from the United States or some foreign country. It is important that minority participation in foreign companies operating in Canada should be open to Canadians. There are obvious reasons why Canadians should be able to affect, to some extent at least, the operation and direction of affairs of all companies in Canada. The more companies that are controlled by Canadians themselves, naturally the happier we will be. But where that is not so, there certainly should be provision for participation by Canadians in all companies in this country.


Actually, at present minority Canadian participation in foreign controlled subsidiaries is discouraged by our own laws. These are recommendations which we have already discussed at different times in this house in detail. I want to summarize some of these subjects which have been discussed here and elsewhere because the impact of our own laws upon investment by Canadians in our own activities is one of the things that have a very great bearing upon the situation which has developed in this country. We have been told that Canadians are unwilling to take risks with their money; that is not so. It is utterly untrue. Canadians are prepared to take risks along with others. Canadians, however, have not found the same opportunities and the same encouragement as others because our own laws are not as beneficial to those who take risks of certain kinds.
May I review some of the ways in which the laws do act contrary to our own interests in this respect:
1.	Canadian tax laws should be changed to eliminate the tax penalty which a British or United States company must suffer when it allows Canadians to own a substantial minority interest in a wholly owned Canadian subsidiary.
2.	The incentive to non-residents to operate in Canada as foreign corporations rather than as subsidiary companies incorporated in Canada should be removed.
3.	There should be stronger incentives in the Income Tax Act for investment companies to invest solely in Canadian equity stocks.
4.	Succession duty laws should be amended to make it easier for Canadian families to maintain control of their businesses.
5.	The method of taxing Canadian oil companies should be changed so that the Canadian operator is not at a disadvantage in competition with United States operators in the Canadian oil fields, as he now is.
6.	Tax deductions should be permitted in respect of research expenditures which will encourage our own research in every field.
I do not intend to review these subjects in detail. It is not possible within the time at my disposal to do so. These cover a vast field. Certain it is, however, Canadian government policy should be designed to give Canadians as favourable a competitive basis for operation as is possible, and1 it should be extended to every possible case where Canadians invest. It certainly should be extended to Canadians as much as or more than it is to the foreign investors no matter where the investors may come from. That is the least that Canadians should expect from their government.

Now, may I speak, and only briefly, of this unfavourable trade balance with the United States which amounted last year to $839,996,794. This enormous amount is one that we cannot disregard. Figures released for the first five months of 1956 indicate that it is likely this unfavourable balance will exceed $1 billion for the current year; that is something to which the Canadian government must give attention. It certainly should be Canadian policy to balance our trade as much as possible and not place ourselves in so precarious a position in relation to any one nation, no matter how friendly that nation may be. We must not place all our eggs in one basket, either in regard to trade or in regard to any other aspect of our economy.
There are many aspects of this unfavourable trade balance which call for our consideration. It is only possible to support such an unusual situation because of the heavy flow of investment money into Canada from the United States. That has made it possible for us to buy many things that we require and undoubtedly many advantages have flowed from those purchases, but it has also limited some of the advantages of the investment which has been made.
Another subject which must be borne in mind is the upward trend in the export of raw materials since the end of the second world war. That has steadily increased. At the same time, the proportion of fully manufactured goods in our exports has been declining. In 1946, 51-8 per cent of all our industrial exports from Canada were in fully manufactured form. In 1954, they had been reduced to 39-8 per cent. At the same time the percentage of fully manufactured goods in our imports has been steadily rising. In 1946, 66-8 per cent of our imports were fully manufactured, while in 1954, 75-6 per cent were fully manufactured. This gives a picture of growing dependence upon outside manufacture which is not consistent with our remarkable position; it is not consistent with the fact that we have every one of the known sources of industrial energy in large quantity and that we have great resources of raw materials beyond the dreams of most countries of the world today.
Nothing that I have said is an argument against foreign investment on the one hand, or the export of resources on the other. It is an argument that in the laws which govern the results of investment, and in the use of our resources, Canadian interests should at all times be protected and encouraged. That will not limit legitimate investment in any way. At the same time our export policies should be related to our own needs
9, 1956
Natural Resources-Development for the future and the desirability of processing as much as we can of our own raw materials in Canada to give employment to new millions of Canadian workers.
These problems pose a question to which all Canadians must be prepared to give an answer one way or another. Do we believe in Canada as a national entity? Do we believe that it is worth while that the people living in this country in the years ahead shall continue to be Canadians with full and effective control over a strong, prosperous and vigorous country? I am sure that it is the wish of Canadians, and I am sure that Canadians want policies which will make that result certain.
We recognize the constitutional division of responsibility, but this government must assume responsibility for guiding policies in regard to international trade. Canadian expansion under as great a measure of Canadian control as is consistent with our national aspirations should be the policy supported by every one of us.
The question before us is simple but vitally important. Are we going to be satisfied with a quick cash return for capital assets which can never be replaced, or are we going to plan privately and publicly for the highest possible use of our own raw materials in Canada under long-term plans of development and conservation? Are we going to be hewers and diggers in large measure for a great and friendly neighbour who will then sell the finished products back to us after the most profitable employment has been created for their own people, or are we going to make the processed and finished articles that we need here in Canada in factories broadly based across the whole of our country to use the materials and resources which providence has entrusted to our care?
I think the answer to these questions is of vital concern to every Canadian. It is of equal concern to our farmers and industrial workers and investors, because the broad prosperity of the Canadian people will depend upon what we do. I have not spoken today about the great production of our agricultural areas. We all know of that. We know that one of our problems is the surplus production; we know that there is nothing so important to the farmer in Canada today as larger consuming markets within this country to provide the ready outlet for the goods that can be produced on our farms in far larger quantities than are being produced today. I think the appropriate answer is clear. I think we should decide that as Canadians we will process our raw materials to the greatest extent that is a practical possibility and in that way create highly paid
5780	HOUSE OF
Natural Resources-Development employment for many new millions of Canadians in the years ahead, that will create more markets for an extended production in Canada in every field.
We all share the satisfaction in the growth and development that has already taken place. But this is only a promise of what can happen. Government policies should encourage the development of our own resources, should promote the processing of those resources in Canada, should correct our unfavourable trade balance, should assure the participation by Canadians in the development and processing of our resources, and should assure opportunity and employment for all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific wherever they may live.
Along with the bright picture that we see in so many centres in Canada today, there are unhappy pictures which no Canadian should ignore. I think many of us have seen the extreme poverty which exists in some parts of this country and which has not been alleviated by the developments that have taken place here. It must be the concern of all Canadians to spread this rich opportunity across our broad land and by the combined efforts of our people make sure that it is not only for some Canadians that these advantages accrue but that the development of those incredible opportunities is truly for the benefit of all Canadians wherever they may live, whatever their occupation may be and whatever part of Canada they call their home.
My firm conviction is that if we adopt a sensible Canada first policy which strengthens our own country we shall then be in a position to make our greatest contribution to international friendship and international cooperation. Upon our own strength will depend the value of our contribution to the joint efforts which are being made for the advancement of civilization throughout the world.
We are indeed a very fortunate people living in a very fortunate land. We are now at the dawn of one of the brightest days which ever opened out before the people of any nation. But it is not only of today but of tomorrow, and of the many other tomorrows, that we should be thinking at this time. We can gain much wealth in a short time for a limited number of people, or we can spread prosperity, security and happiness across the whole land, depending on the course that we follow.
We wish to be good friends of all nations; that goes without saying. But first of all we wish to be strong within our own boundaries and within every part inside our boundaries. With the right policies today Canada can have a population of at least 30 million people within the next 25 years,


and by the end of the century we should have at least 75 million people and be a great and prosperous world power.
I have said this before, but I repeat it from deep conviction. For the Canadians of today and of tomorrow this can indeed be the beginning of Canada's golden age. Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada, encourage more processing of those resources in Canada, correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances, foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources, and promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate in this circumstance, one is under some disadvantage. Not having had an opportunity to make preparation and marshal the necessary material facts, one is perhaps unable to do justice to a topic of this importance. However, I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) this afternoon in moving this resolution and in the address which introduced it has placed before the house a great deal of material and has advanced many arguments that will appeal to members on all sides of the house. I agree with him that Canada should be on the verge of still greater expansion.
When I say that we should be on the verge of still greater expansion it is because over the last half century or so we have seen a tremendous growth both in the development of our resources and indeed in our population. I can look back now over almost a half a century since I came to this country as an immigrant. I recall the prairies as they were then, wide open spaces, the homesteaders building their sod shacks and in many instances still breaking the land with oxen. When one sees what has developed in that agricultural area over the last 45 or 50 years one realizes what expansion can be achieved in the years to come in all parts of Canada.
One has only to move from one side of this country to the other to realize the variety of our resources as well as the beauty of the land in which we live and the diversity of the people who inhabit the land, people of diverse origins. Our English-speaking population today is not wholly Anglo-Saxon, but intermingled with the people who inherited the English language from their forebears are those who have come to us from other

countries and have been integrated into the English-speaking part of Canada. We also have the French-speaking population which has grown and expanded and assisted so materially in both the industrial and cultural development of the land in which we live. Consequently when one projects his mind 25, 50, 75 or 100 years hence one begins to see a picture of what this country may be in the years to come.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition has placed before us some considerations to which we should pay some attention in this parliament at the present time. It is quite true that the development-or shall I use the word "exploitation"-of many of our natural resources has fallen under the control of interests that are not Canadian, whose only thought in the exploitation of those resources is the making of a maximum amount of profit and return on the capital they have invested in our land. It seems to me that while we do welcome capital from outside the country to assist in the development of our resources, we in this parliament, and perhaps more particularly the members in the provincial legislatures, have an obligation to see that this development is planned in order that the maximum benefit may accrue to Canada today and to Canadians in years to come.
I noticed the Leader of the Opposition used words to this effect. He said what we need is a national program consciously planned, and I agree with him. We in this group have long held that if we are to develop this country along the right lines we must have sound national economic planning. By national economic planning I do not mean that it must be done by the central authority, but that under the leadership of the federal authority the provincial governments in cooperation with the federal authority should be planning the utilization of our resources not only for today but also for the years to come.
When we move across this country we can see the extent to which our resources are being not developed but exploited. I have our great forest resources in mind at the moment. Had I known this debate was to come up this afternoon I might have looked up some information I have at home on this subject. About two weeks ago a timber expert from a Scandinavian country made a statement as he departed from Canada. He had visited this country for some months, and in his investigation of the manner in which these resources in Canada were being utilized he had taken jobs at various lumber camps without indicating his real interest in Canadian forestry.

Natural Resources-Development
When he left he made a statement to the effect that he had been very interested in seeing the vast forest resources Canada has, he had been interested in having an opportunity to investigate the manner in which they were being exploited, and then he went on to say that he knew of nowhere in the world where the forest resources were being as wastefully denuded as they are in our country at the present time. He also went on to say, of course, that our vast forest resources were not inexhaustible, and that at the rate we are cutting down the trees and not replacing them under any conscious plan the time would come when Canada would be without these great forest resources.
One has only to remember what happened in the United States some 50, 60 or 100 years ago to be aware of what results from a lack of planning. One has only to travel through Minnesota, Wisconsin or Michigan, which at one time were the great forested areas of the United States, to realize that the heritage of scrub, sand and rock, in Minnesota particularly, has resulted because the people of that day and generation failed to safeguard and properly utilize the great resources which once covered those vast areas of the United States.
Coming in a little closer to home, one only has to drive up and down the Ottawa valley to realize that 100 years ago this valley was the scene of one of the finest stands of white pine in North America. One has only to go to the archives and other places to see pictures of the Ottawa and Rideau rivers of 75 or 100 years ago to see the rafts of mighty timber that were coming down. Today you can drive up and down this Ottawa valley and except for an isolated tree here and there you can find no descendants of those great trees which once covered the area.
What has happened in Michigan? What has happened in Wisconsin? What has happened in Minnesota? What has happened in this Ottawa valley, still beautiful indeed with the scrub bush which now covers it but denuded of the great forests which once added to its glory. Without conservation and planned use the same will happen in British Columbia, in the northern parts of the prairie provinces, in Ontario and Quebec and indeed in the maritimes, where already many great forests have been lost to this generation. Thus we can readily realize what may happen in the future. I think the generation which is exploiting our forests is doing an injustice to the generations which will follow.
What we need in connection with the development of our resources is a national

Natural Resources-Development plan to be applied as we use our forest resources. I give this as an example because they are replaceable, and are not like minerals where once you take them out of the ground you have nothing left but a hole. There are possibilities of replacing our forest areas so that future generations may have the resources upon which they can build industry of various sorts and types and thus be enabled to be happy and prosperous.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition spoke of other lands where once upon a time there had been great and prosperous cities. There had been cities in the Sahara desert, in Mesopotamia where according to tradition the garden of Eden was situated between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Until comparatively recent times, until indeed some new irrigation projects were undertaken, the valleys of these historic rivers were nothing but deserts of driven sand. The same thing applies, of course, to North Africa. Anyone who has visited North Africa will have seen the hillsides in Palestine which were once the vineyards of that area and which are now merely eroded terraces of rock. The soil has gone and nothing can grow there. One then realizes what human beings can do to the resources of a land if there is no proper policy of planning and conservation.
If we are to have proper water resources, if we are to have water to irrigate the parched lands of the prairies, then we must maintain the cover on the mountain sides so that water will flow, not in great floods sweeping everything before them but more gently during the season of the year when it is needed for irrigation purposes. Linked with the preservation of our forests is the conservation of water, for irrigation purposes particularly. That is linked again with the conservation of soil. I have already mentioned Mesopotamia, the Sahara desert and the Kalahari desert and indeed parts of India where teeming populations once lived and grew the necessary cereals and other crops to maintain themselves. They are now deserts because the soil was improperly tilled and improperly cultivated.
Many of us remember the drifting soil on the prairies of North America, and in referring to the prairies of North America I include the prairies of Nebraska and Kansas as well as those of Alberta and Saskatchewan, in those dreadful years of drought. I think we have learned a lesson that we shall never forget. I have been happy to note that the farmers on the Canadian prairies have taken note and have changed their methods of cultivation. Only recently during a very dry period with high winds on
[Mr. Coldwell.l

the prairies I saw very few spots where the soil was blowing as it would have done 25 or 30 years ago under the same circumstances. This was true because the agricultural population of that region had taken to heart the lessons of the windy dry years of the 1930's and changed their methods of cultivation so they conserved the soil for their own use and indeed for that of future generations.
As the Leader of the Opposition has said, not only have we forests, not only have we soil, not only have we water resources, we have resources in the water in our fisheries both inland in the great lakes and in the northern regions where numerous fishermen catch fish in the lakes to make their living, as well as along the coasts of Canada. The conservation of salmon on the Pacific coast, the replacement of salmon on the Atlantic coast and the general supervision now given to the fishing industry is a form of planning, a form of planned development which could be applied in another way, of course, in co-operation with the provinces to our forest and other resources of this country.
Then we have the tremendous resources of the Canadian shield. Almost every kind of mineral is to be found there. Then in the far north we have the huge deposits of iron ore to which reference has been made already this afternoon. But we must not forget that these are wasting resources. While perhaps we cannot foresee at the moment when the minerals of that vast area will be exhausted, one day perchance that may come about. As has been suggested this afternoon, we should try to do what we can as a parliament, co-operating with the legislatures of the provinces, to see to it that as much of those mineral resources as possible is utilized and developed for the building of Canadian industry and the prosperity of our Canadian people.
I am not suggesting that we should act like a dog in the manger and prevent the flow of raw materials to industry elsewhere, but I do suggest that that flow is greater than it should be, and that we should be doing much more of the processing of those raw materials and those minerals in our own country. When we think of the diversity of our mineral development over the past few years and the remarkable discoveries of oil that have been made in the province of Alberta and are now being made in the province of Saskatchewan, the province of Manitoba and indeed the province of British Columbia, we realize that there we have a great resource that should help to build up our Canadian economy.

It is quite true that because of the enormous amounts of capital that were required for the exploration and development of this oil resource, the control has fallen very largely under the domination of several great United States oil companies, but in the further development of this great resource we should do all we can to see to it that as great a control as possible is maintained in Canada, and certainly that no ^foreign corporation should be able to say to the Canadian people, "This is my oil" or "This is my gas, and unless you utilize it as I decree I am not going to allow you to utilize it at all." That has been said, and that is the kind of thing this parliament and our provincial legislatures should view with some misgiving and should seek by proper legislation to rectify and bring under the greater control of our own Canadian people.
We have tremendous resources newly discovered, which already are establishing great industries. When one goes, for example, to the city of Edmonton, a city that I knew nearly half a century ago-

As my friend from Cape Breton South says, nylon stockings originate largely in the coal fields of Nova Scotia, Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and other parts of Canada. So we have an obligation to the future generations of Canadians to safeguard these great resources.
This afternoon the Leader of the Opposition mentioned the human resources. Without adequate development of our human resources, of course, we cannot properly develop our mineral and other natural resources. I think Canada has not done nearly enough in the realm of education and in the encouragement of young men and young women to take various courses in our universities. I am not one of those who believe we should say to every young man and woman, "Take a scientific course or a technical course in our colleges and universities." Far from it; I would tell every young man and woman who wants to take a scientific or technical course in our universities first of all to take the arts course and get a broad picture of life that will serve them well in any field of endeavour they may undertake in the years to come.
We have not done enough in any of these fields of education. Of course I have often said that without interference with the control of education by the provinces this parliament should be making grants for education, should be encouraging in every possible way the expansion of our universities and giving encouragement to all our young men and women who have the ability to take a higher education. As I said some time ago, one of the great satisfactions I had when I was in the United Kingdom two years ago was to go back to my old college and to the other educational institutions in that country and be told that, contrary to what it was when

Natural Resources-Development I was young, when my parents had to sacrifice tremendously to give me the education I got, today no boy or girl with ability would be denied higher education right through to the university in Britain, because of the scholarships and the bursaries and the grants to the universities made by the government of the United Kingdom. Of course it is a little simpler there because they have a unitary system of government, while here we have, of course, a federal system; but I think it could be worked out here between the provinces and the federal authorities to the satisfaction and the advantage of the country.
Stemming out of that, of course, is the need for research. Until very recently not a great deal of research was done in this country. I think the national research council has done a magnificent job. The national research council gave an impetus to research in this country. It was a public institution but, very fortunately, many of our great industries have followed suit and are now paying much more attention to research than they were a few years ago, although I do not think they are paying sufficient attention yet. More research must be encouraged in our country and that means, of course, that we must have more young men and women prepared to enter into the fields of research in all phases.
If we are going to do all these things we cannot adopt an attitude of laissez-faire. We cannot leave it merely to individual corporations and individual persons to undertake all this. We have to have some conscious planning, some conscious economic and social planning, in which we, of course, as a party believe. That does not mean that everything has to be done under public ownership and public control. I think we learned many lessons during the years of depression and subsequently. In a modern society leadership must be given by public organizations. But in a modern mixed economy there is room for private enterprise which will help to develop the resources of the country in order to give to our people a better standard of living; and most of all, of course, there is need for the organization of co-operative associations of various types and sorts to distribute as well as to produce many of the things that make life worth living.
I am therefore going to leave the matter at that, Mr. Speaker. I want to say that we agree that if we are to develop our resources intelligently, as the Leader of the Opposition said, there must be a national program consciously planned. If it is consciously planned, the federal authority must give leadership. It may not undertake it wholly itself but rather must do so in co-operation with the provinces, because the natural resources of the country
[Mr. Coldwell.l

are controlled by the provinces of Canada. If we do this, I am convinced that over the years we shall see developed in this country a vigorous and prosperous population which can look forward in the years to come to contributing not only to the welfare of the people of this country itself, but generally to the welfare of the world.
Let us not forget this fact Mr. Speaker. This can be done under the guidance of our democratic institutions. Today democratic institutions are being challenged as they have never been challenged before. The totalitarian countries tell us of what they are able to do in developing their resources. They are trying to demonstrate to some of the underprivileged people who one day will probably decide the fate of the world that they can do better than the democracies. I am certain that under our democratic institutions we can do better than they can.
However, the outcome depends on the energy we put into the doing of this job. If we want to win over these people of the world who are being told by the totalitarian countries, "We have achieved much in a short time", we too must achieve much in a short time in our country. We can do that. We can develop our resources. As the Leader of the Opposition suggested this afternoon, we can remove the spots-there are many of them, and some of them are quite large spots-where poverty, misery and disease exist. We have the resources. All we need is the will; and given the opportunity, I believe the Canadian people have the will to do this job.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is to the advantage of Canada that occasionally the members of this house stop to take a look at the over-all policy that guides the development and growth of our great country. I think it is wise occasionally to place before the house a motion such as that which has been moved this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, which gives us all a chance to express our point of view. It helps to focus attention upon our resources and how best they can be developed in the interests of all the people of this country and of the country itself. I am therefore extremely glad to have this opportunity of saying a word in connection with the speech made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition and the amendment he moved.
I could not help feeling how great a change has taken place in the thinking of many members of this house in 10 years. When I came into the House of Commons 10 years ago, everybody seemed to be quite enthusiastic about internationalism and the prospect

of finding the answer to our local problems by surrendering our economic defences, giving them away. Now we have come around full circle to a degree of economic nationalism that I would not have believed possible in that length of time. I congratulate the members of the house who have already spoken on the fact that they have grown older and wiser and that, with their grey hairs, they have come to understand that there is no answer to our local problems in the surrender of our economic defences, that we cannot look to internationalism to solve our own problems.
I was interested especially this afternoon in listening to a good many of the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition, with which I agree. I am going to deal just briefly with some of them. To begin with, I must say that I would have been much more impressed with many of them had 1 seen some evidence a few years ago of an inclination on the part of his followers in this house to take a stand that was possible at that time, namely a stand for retaining our economic defences and against some pernicious things that have happened to lose those defences for us.
