I listen to my hon. friend and he often says something worth while. But he kept a very strange silence back in 1945, at a time when he should have been speaking up on something worth while instead of a lot of the piffle that he often talks.
My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition said we are not manufacturing nearly enough here in Canada. I agree. I believe I am right when I say that last year Canada imported a greater dollar value of finished goods than any other country in the world, irrespective of its population. I think that statistic should soak in. If it is not true, I should like to have the facts presented. I believe it is true. It indicates that we in Canada have failed to develop our industries as they might have been developed.
Of course we have not done all we can in industrial expansion. I agree with that
Natural Resources-Development statement. But the question is, what is the answer? I believe that one of the great statesmen of Canada back in the late nineteenth century made the statement that the great need of that time in Canada was for transportation, and he repeated it; transportation, transportation, transportation.
We have our transportation fairly well developed now, Mr. Speaker. I believe the greatest need in Canada today is markets.
I believe therein lies the answer to this question of industrialization in Canada. However, we cannot expect the total market of Canada to be available to our industrialists until we make absolutely sure that our people have the purchasing power with which to buy what has been produced. There is no question about that. Of course many people will laugh and emit those funny cackles which indicate that they do not know much about the situation and have not given much thought to it.
The greatest problem in Canada today with respect to industrial inducement or encouragement is that of getting purchasing power into the hands of the people. Until we make certain that they have purchasing power that is equal to our productive capacity, we are not going to get the industrial expansion w* ought to have.
Now, we say that we are not manufacturing enough in Canada. But where are the markets; that is the big question. Our industrialists are asking that question. The Canadian people have got into the habit of buying in the United States. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out last year they bought from the United States a billion dollars worth of goods more than the people of the United States bought from Canada. We have got into the pattern of buying in the United States. Why is that? The big reason, of course, is that the people of Canada find they can buy a good many things cheaper down there than they can buy them here. The Leader of the Opposition said in his speech, and certainly indicated in his amendment, that one of the reasons has been that in Canada we have not paid enough attention to this whole problem of taxes.
For a great many years we have imposed upon commodities not only sales taxes but also certain excise taxes. These taxes have increased costs and they have, to a very large measure, discouraged our Canadian people from buying things made in Canada. As a consequence a great many of them regularly go down into the United States and buy to the limit of the customs allowance. They bring those goods into Canada. The Minister of Finance ought to take a look

Natural Resources-Development some time at the possibilities in the purchases by the people of Canada in the United States. If a large proportion of them take it into their heads to go to the United States every four months, as they can, and buy and bring back into Canada a hundred dollars worth of goods duty free, then let the minister figure out how much it would amount to.
Our people, Mr. Speaker, have got into the habit of buying in the United States. The consequence is that we have a trade unbalance. The question I have to ask myself is, how in the world can this pattern be changed? There is one way in which it can be changed, and that is by making it more profitable for the people of Canada to buy Canadian made goods. I have in my hand something which is pertinent to the case. Here is a little column, a short one, which indicates something of the problem at any rate. I cannot say whether or not the figures are exactly right, but it indicates the extent of the problem. It is headed, "Hidden Taxes Chisel from Cradle to Grave", and is written by Fred Edge in Liberty magazine. This is what it says:
Not long ago a Winnipeg triend of mine bought an automobile for $2,600. "How much," he asked the salesman, "am I paying in taxes on the actual price of this car?"
The salesman had to admit he didn't know, and wasn't too interested. Like most Canadians, he accepted government taxes as a part of purchase-written into the price tag in invisible ink. My friend did some checking on his own. He found: Sales tax on his car was slightly more than $170. Excise tax was about $280. Approximate total tax: $450!
Each year, Canadians make out their income tax, mutter briefly over how much tax they pay on their salary-and promptly forget taxes until next year. Few people realize they pay staggering taxes every time they buy anything from shoes to toothpaste. The tax they pay makes the average man's income tax look minor.
Cigarette smokers who smoke just one package of cigarettes a day are paying $62.05 a year in tax to the dominion government-or 17 cents on each package. The man who buys a bottle of Canadian made rye for $4 is paying roughly 84 cents for the rye and $3.16 to the provincial and dominion governments. The sales tax alone on a pound of coffee or tea costing $1.10 is 6 cents; a pair of $15 shoes carries 95 cents sales tax; tax on a 40 cent tube of toothpaste is 2 cents.
The iniquitous hidden tax, borne by Canadians from the moment of birth-both pins and diapers carry an unseen sales tax-follows right to the grave. The government last year pocketed roughly $1,000,000 on the hidden sales tax on coffins.
Now, as I say, I have not checked the figures that were used in this article. What I do say is that the whole article indicates as least one facet of the problem. As long as we make it unattractive for Canadians to buy Canadian goods, then certainly they are going to seek their purchases elsewhere. It 

is only natural that they will go to the United States and buy as much as they can bring back duty free. Sometimes they are able to buy things in the United States, pay the taxes and still beat us here in Canada.
In his amendment the Leader of the Opposition mentioned something about taking action in connection with taxes so we can make things much more attractive in Canada. We have got to expand our markets, and it does not matter how much well planned immigration we attract into Canada; that will not solve the problem unless we are going to do something about prices. We do have an answer to this price problem, and we can get along without imposing these price-pyramiding excise and sales taxes that put us behind the eight ball when it comes to the question of competing with other countries in the matter of trade.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke of foreign financial control of a very large percentage of Canadian resources. I followed him as he spoke about those things and he failed to say anything about the answer to that problem, nor did he enlighten the house as to when and how the roots of that condition were put out. He did not say, for example, that beginning with the administration of Sir John A. Macdonald and right down to our own day, the governments of Canada and all the provinces have given away large blocks of Canada's resources, alienated them from the crown and alienated them also from Canadian control. In the old days it used to be the fashion to reward political heelers for services rendered to the party, and when a party got into power they would hand over large blocks of our resources to those people for exploitation. This has not stopped yet, Mr. Speaker, yet we talk about foreign control. We have seen something of this situation in our own province. I am going to say that the Leader of the Opposition was not completely correct when he said that foreign financial control has arisen simply from the fact that investment in Canada offers such rich returns.
I am sure that everybody is aware of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway, the C. and D. Corporation and the Hudson Bay Company, as well as other big concerns, were given outright very large blocks of our resources, our mineral rights. During the years they have taken control of those outside of Canada to a very large degree, removed them from the control of the government of Canada. I am not blaming this government for that. It happened that when we came into office in Alberta in 1935 we discovered that slightly over 50 per cent of the subsurface rights, minerals and oil, had

been alienated from the crown and the people, by deed of gift, by sale or by some other means that we have not been able to find out. That left us less than 50 per cent controlled in the interests of the people.
Well, we sat down and thought about the situation for some time, and tried to figure out means by which we could see that the rest of the resources that remained unalienated could be developed in the interests of all the people. I believe we succeeded in laying down a policy that would do it. We decided then and there that one of the important points that we had to observe was that not one square foot of any of those resources remaining in the possession of the crown for and on behalf of the people should be further alienated, and we have stayed with that policy to this day. Not one square foot has been sold or given away.
We adopted a policy of leases, rentals and royalties under which we sought to attract people who would come and invest their risk capital in a lease controlled by the crown. The ownership of those resources was to remain vested in the crown and be administered for and on behalf of the people. Always the control, in a circumstance like that, will be in the government, not outside. As a consequence we have gone forward in the development of our resources in the province of Alberta. That portion which remained unalienated has been developed for the people. They own it. But the development has taken place under a process of private enterprise, and there have been no alienations in the last 21 years.
That is one way by which these things can be accomplished, by which we can establish the foundations for a true Canada first policy; but we cannot establish a Canada first policy if we are going further to alienate our resources from the crown and give them away to others to exploit, under which plan Canadians will find themselves under the complete domination of foreign countries.
Well, we dealt with the situation and we started this, Mr. Speaker, in an effort to build up our industrialization. We had as our objective the bringing about of a balance as nearly as possible between our agriculture and our industry, and I think we have fairly well succeeded; but we had to resort to some very interesting means. One of those means was to intensify the effort to sell our Alberta people on the purchase of Alberta goods. We did so by using a very interesting form of local purchasing power and a process of bonusing Alberta made goods. It did intensify industrialization; it did succeed in focusing the attention of the people of Alberta on the need for buying Alberta goods. While we
Natural Resources-Development were not trying to discriminate against any other province or any other country, we felt the absolute need of doing what we could to build up industry in Alberta, and I think we have fairly well succeeded in that.
I believe we have to start there; we have to start on a broader scale to see to it that our resources are kept in the ownership and control of the people of Canada. That is perfectly correct. It can be said, of course, that the oil industry to a very large extent is financed by people outside of Canada. I do not know whether it is 90 per cent, 80 per cent, or what it is; nobody knows. But, Mr. Speaker, let me point out this fact. It does not make any difference, or not so much difference at any rate, where the investment risk capital comes from so long as the ownership remains vested in the people of a province of this country, and so long as control is exercised by the governments of the provinces to see to it that the development takes place for and on behalf of the people and they get the benefits. There is no question about that. That is what we have tried to do, and I think we have succeeded to a remarkable degree.
While there are people who inveigh against the big oil companies, yet the big oil companies are not in a position to dictate what shall be done with the oil, the gas or any other of our resources in the province. The policy we have followed does not allow that, and I think it can be demonstrated without question that this is so.
My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition spoke briefly about the trade deficit of a billion dollars with the United States last year. That trade deficit, Mr. Speaker, has developed very largely as a consequence of our failure 11 years ago to stand up against the pernicious international arrangement that was advocated and adopted in this house. At that time we in this corner of the house pointed out that if Canada became a party to the Bretton Woods agreement it would throw our whole trade arrangements into complete-well, confusion, to say the least. We point out then, Mr. Speaker, how Bretton Woods favoured creditor nations like the United States, and how it did not place upon the United States, or upon any other creditor nation, the responsibility of balancing its trade by the acceptance of goods from other countries. But it did place upon the debtor nations that responsibility. It introduced an international gold standard, and gave the creditor nations the right to sit back and demand gold or United States dollars in payment of trade balances. Now, where in the world is the gold to come from?

Natural Resources-Development
My hon. friend was not in the house at that time, it is true. He was in Toronto as leader of the government of Ontario. Had he been here I am interested to know what he would have done about it. His followers here did not do anything. They joined with the government of the day and with the C.C.F. in voting us down, in steamrollering us because we stood out against this pernicious international agreement under which we gave away our economic defences and made possible the very thing that now takes place, where the United States refuses to balance her trade, or even to try to balance her trade, by buying from other countries with United States dollars an equal amount or nearly equal amount of what those countries buy from the United States.
Canada sits back today complacently and allows those trade deficits to pile up. We do have an inclination on the part of people having capital in the United States to come in here and invest in our resources; otherwise we would be in a pickle. What in the world we would do about those trade balances if we did not have this investment I do not know. Therefore 1 say I would have been much more impressed with what the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon if he had said we ought to set out at once to correct this situation. There is an escape clause in the Bretton Woods agreement. It would be possible for us to get out of it, and I think we should be talking here about the necessity-in fact it is a moral obligation- on the part of the United States to try to balance her trade by buying in other countries an amount equal to what other countries buy in the United States.
How can they get the dollars to balance their trade if they buy in the United States and the United States does not buy from them? And so we suffer this terrific trade imbalance very largely as a consequence of the developments of the last 10 years, and my hon. friends over here have nobody to blame but themselves, along with the other parties in this house.

May I refer for a few moments to the terms of the amendment which, it seems to me, consists of four different propositions. The first is:
. . . the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our natural resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada.
I think that is quite correct, Mr. Speaker.
I think we all agree with it. I believe even the government would agree that that is so. They may say, "We already have it". I do


not believe they have. I do believe that through dominion-provincial taxation, financial arrangements and conferences of various kinds we might develop such a policy so that our natural resources will be developed for the maximum benefit of all the people in Canada, but you cannot do it until you lay down a policy similar to that which we have adopted and have used so successfully for 21 years in the province of Alberta.
The second important thing he suggests is the adoption of a national development policy that will encourage greater processing of our natural resources in Canada. Again may I say I agree with that, but I would point out that until such time as we clear away the taxation and other disabilities that militate against the popularity of Canadian goods, until we see to it that our people have the purchasing power with which they can buy what we produce, then there is not much use talking about encouraging the processing of these resources in Canada. We have to make it possible for our industry to compete with other nations in the world of trade, and we cannot do it by any pious statements of hope.
He suggests that we should correct the present serious unfavourable trade balances. I have already said I would have been much more impressed by that part of his amendment if the hon. gentleman had told us where they stand with respect to the Bretton Woods international agreement and the things it has done for Canada.
He also suggests we have to foster wider financial participation by Canadians in the development of our resources. Once again that is a very desirable thing to do, but how it can be accomplished is another question. You cannot force people to do this. Instead, it has to be done by other processes. Certainly it is a desirable goal.
His last suggestion concerns a policy to promote greater opportunity and employment for a steadily increasing population. Yes, that is perfectly correct.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say again all of that depends on whether or not we succeed in bringing our purchasing power into balance with our productive capacity. If we do that I think we will have laid the foundation, but until we do all the rest of these things are nothing but pious hopes.

speechtext:
Well, if it is politeness it is a new departure in this house on the part of the government. I think the politeness might have been better demonstrated by the government in acquainting the house with its views on this very important amendment and the policy it enunciates and invites the house now to pass upon. I suppose the government is waiting to be furnished with speeches to be read after they have been prepared for them by their officials. One would have hoped that they would have had something to say at this stage of the debate before a second round of opposition speakers should have commenced.
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this amendment is not just a passing issue. This amendment states an abiding objective of policy of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and it touches upon subjects to which all Canadians-and not least of all this house

need to devote some hard thinking and serious attention. We approach this question not on a negative or merely emotional basis but on a positive and constructive basis. We are advocating a national development policy.
At the outset I wish to touch on two aspects of this matter to set our approach to this question in perspective. The first relates to the role of government. We consider that the function of government in relation to national development policy is to create a climate favourable to individual enterprise, and it is within the sphere of government or public enterprise in carrying forward its public works, enterprises, projects, expenditures and policies to do so with goals in view such as those stated in the amendment.
The second general observation relates to the constitution of this country. Under our constitution the development of our natural resources falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but in the development of those resources there is a fruitful field for co-operation between the dominion and the provincial governments; and then, of course, there is the vast field assigned by the constitution exclusively to the federal authority, namely jurisdiction over trade and commerce of an interprovincial or international character.
The development of our resources, sir, is a subject to stir the imagination of any Canadian. Providence has blessed this country with a vast store of natural resources.
9, 1956	5789
Natural Resources-Development In the custody and use of those resources we Canadians must have due regard for the need of conserving them and for the need of replacing wasting resources; and there are important fields in which the federal authority has an opportunity of contributing in a significant measure to the development of our resources. I mention in passing just two great projects which we of Her Majesty's loyal opposition have long advocated against the determination of the government not to have any part of them.
I refer, of course, to the South Saskatchewan irrigation dam against which the Prime Minister and the Liberal party have firmly set their faces notwithstanding what the Minister of Agriculture continues to say on the subject out in the west, and also to the Beechwood project in New Brunswick, which promises great benefits to that part of Canada and which the federal government refused to assist even to the very limited extent of guaranteeing the bonds of the province of New Brunswick issued for the purpose of financing that beneficent project.
We wish to see measures of that kind undertaken by the federal authority, measures that will be of benefit to all parts of Canada. The Leader of the Opposition this afternoon referred to the fact that the postwar increase in purchasing power in Canada has not been evenly distributed, and pointed out that in the maritime provinces purchasing power has not kept pace with individual purchasing power in other parts of this country. There is a need of development of secondary industry in the Atlantic provinces and in the west.
The federal government had a glowing opportunity to carry forward that process of development of secondary industry during the war and in this period of building up our defences during the past six years. That opportunity has been largely thrown away. A valuable opportunity has been lost, an opportunity that would have contributed much to repairing the disadvantage under which geography has placed those parts of the country and thereby could have helped to distribute the benefits as well as the cost of confederation.
There is a fruitful field also for the processing of more of our natural resources within the boundaries of Canada. We as a Conservative party do not regard the development of our resources as the equivalent of the export of those resources in raw form to other countries. Today Canada is exporting heavily from her raw resources and those resources, we need to remind ourselves, are not inexhaustible. In a measure we are depleting our storehouse of resources. We

Natural Resources-Development are not doing it as we might in order to provide opportunities to Canadians in the processing and fabrication of those materials into the finished products in Canada.
The Paley report in the United States had an extremely sobering effect in that country on those who thought that the be-all and end-all was the development of raw resources. That report, in drawing attention to the threatened exhaustion of many of the natural resources in the United States, has a lesson for Canada. It is not only that our resources may be depleted, but that between 1950 and 1975 the United States will need to quadruple its imports of industrial materials. The materials which the United States is going to require in that period and later happen to be largely the kind of resources that we have in Canada. To an increasing degree therefore the United States is going to be obliged to look to Canada as a supplier of raw materials for the great industrial machine of the United States to process.
We are exporting those raw materials to the United States and are buying back from the United States to a considerable degree the same goods in finished form after United States labour has been expended on their manufacture with benefit to United States workmen. Canadian workmen should have the opportunity to do that work.
We should also remind ourselves that the United States tariff is constructed with the idea of not putting any obstacles in the way of the importation of raw materials for fabrication in the United States, but it does aim to exclude either partly or finished manufactured goods. Generally speaking that tariff rises notably as the degree of manufacture increases, and the duty is low or frequently non-existent on raw materials or some of the simply processed items. The duties are very substantial and sometimes extremely high on manufactured goods. The United States tariff structure is a serious barrier in the way of a natural and desirable avenue of Canadian development, that is to increase the extent of processing and fabrication of our own basic resources.
I wish just to throw out a word of caution on this subject before I go further. Let it not be said that what we are advocating is an embargo upon the export of raw materials to the United States. No, that is not what we are advocating. Indeed, the production of some of our extractive industries-nickel is an example-is such that Canada will not be a consumer of very much of the production, and certainly not a total consumer. As nearly as one can see there will always be a vast production of nickel available for export


which would not be required in the fabrication of manufactured goods in Canada.
In the second place, we do not propose any repudiation or sudden reversal of policies which will deny to those who have entered into contractual arrangements the rights to which they have thereby become entitled. We are not unmindful of the need at the present time to maintain our volume of exports in the face of the very high excess of imports over exports, but we have to consider as a nation what are our objectives in this regard.
A few months ago there appeared before the Gordon royal commission a very eminent Canadian, Mr. Robert Fowler, who is a well known and distinguished Liberal and who spoke for the pulp and paper industry. He submitted to that royal commission that the role for which Canada by nature and destiny was best suited was, as he put it, to be "a hewer of wood and a drawer of water". In other words, he submitted that Canada's economic role was to carve out of our forests and extract from our soil products which should be then exported to the United States. This is what was advocated by a prominent Liberal whose position is recognized by his having been appointed as chairman of a royal commission. I ask, is this government policy?

speechtext: Of course not; it is his personal opinion.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ADOPTION OF NATURAL RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
We should like to have something more in the way of concrete evidence that this is not government policy than simply an offhand remark by the Minister of Finance, who has not chosen to make a speech in the course of this debate. I think it would be a very good thing, now that the Minister of Finance has allowed himself to utter the one sentence he has in this debate, that he should rise and tell us what the government's policy is, because we wish to know. The time for it has come and we do not propose to be put off on this subject any longer.
If you want proof of what can be accomplished in this regard you have only to look at what was accomplished by my leader when he was premier of the province of Ontario by insisting that forest products should be processed in that province instead of being exported in raw form to the United States. The development which has resulted has been remarkable, and is a tribute to his far-sighted policy. There are in Ontario whole communities which owe their existence today, not to mention their prosperity, to the farsighted policies of this kind which he put into effect when he was premier of the province of Ontario.

Let me give another example of commodities in connection with which a good deal could be accomplished, and we have a very recent experience to point to. I refer to aluminum. Canada is a very large producer of aluminum, and much of the aluminum consumed in manufacturing in the United States comes from Canada. Last year there was a serious shortage of aluminum in Canada and the United States, but did the Canadian processors enjoy any benefit from the fact that this is a Canadian product? Did Canadian fabricators and manufacturers have first claim upon the Canadian production of aluminum? No, they did not. They were seriously curtailed. Here is a very apt example of the sort of thing which could be accomplished to the benefit of all Canada if some regard were had for the desirability of fabricating and processing these natural products to a much greater degree in Canada.
I wish to speak on the subject of trade. Our unfavourable trade balance has reached most serious proportions. Indeed, I think it is not too strong to say that it has reached alarming proportions. In 1955 Canada in its trade with the world incurred an over-all trade deficit for the third year in succession. It amounted to $360 million. In 1956 the situation has become more serious still. The daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of July 6 tells us that Canadian commodity imports in the first five months of this year amounted to $2,359,100,000, up $551,800,000 or 30-5 per cent over last year's figures for the same five months. Canadian exports rose only 11-6 per cent, to $1,874,900,000 from $1,680,000,000 last year. For the five months January to May inclusive, the import balance this year aggregated $484,200,000, as compared with an import balance of just $127,300,000 last year. In other words, in our commodity trading with the world our import balance in the first five months of this year was four times as much as it was in the first five months of 1955.
Those are the figures of our over-all trade with the world. What about our trade with the United States? I have drawn attention to the fact that our commodity trade deficit with the whole world is amounting to $100 million per month. We are buying from the world at the rate of $100 million per month more than we are selling; but what about the United States? Here the situation is much more alarming still.
Last year in our commodity trade with the United States we incurred a deficit of $840 million, a deficit greater than any in our history with the exception of one year, namely the year 1947. It was an increase of 40 per cent over the deficit with the United States

Natural Resources-Development in the year 1954. But in the first five months of the year 1956 we are increasing that same deficit with the United States at an alarming rate. Indeed, it is just about double what it was last year for the same period. To an alarming degree we are placing our trading eggs in one basket.
In 1955, continuing a process that was evident in preceding years, Canada drew from the United States 73 per cent of its total imports and only 11-6 per cent from the United Kingdom. Of our exports, 60 per cent went to the United States and only 18 per cent to the United Kingdom. It is evident that we as a country are being drawn more and more into the trading and economic orbit of the United States, and the government seems to be quite indifferent in the face of these facts.
Consider these figures of our trade with the United States for the first five months of this year. In the five months our purchases from the United States amounted to $1,765 million, up 31 per cent from $1,349 million in the first five months of 1955. The result was an import balance for these five months of $625 million as compared with $352,800,000 in 1955. Our excess of purchases from the United States over our sales to the United States is running at the rate of $125 million a month. I think it is time this house and this government took stock of this alarming disproportion in our trade. But when I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce several months ago what the government proposed to do in the face of this situation, which was then becoming apparent, his answer was a glib "nothing". The government has done nothing about it and apparently continues to do nothing about it.
It is facts like these that have led an eminent Canadian economist, Mr. Douglas Gibson, in delivering his presidential address to the annual meeting of the Canadian political science association a few weeks ago, to say:
Certainly in the economic sphere the United States constitutes the only real threat to Canadian independence and it will remain our chief economic preoccupation as far ahead as one can see.
Further on he added:
Even the briefest examination of the facts makes it clear that our ties with the American economy have become closer and more important during the past decade than ever before.
It is an unchallengeable fact, yet the government faces this fact without concern.
Another kind of trade ought to be giving us more concern. We are buying back from the United States processed goods while our exports to her consist largely of raw materials.

The United States is a good neighbour. Let no one misunderstand anything we have to say concerning our trade with the United States. We recognize the burden of leadership that the United States is bearing in the world today. We recognize the burdens that she is carrying for the benefit of all the western world. But Canada's trading relationships with the United States ought to be a matter of very serious concern to every Canadian, as they face us at this time.
We are the best customer the United States has in the world, but we do not always see appreciation of that fact on the part of those who are shaping either administrative or legislative policies at Washington. It is always difficult for other countries who deal with the United States, because of the separation of the administration from the legislative branch of government there.
We Conservatives as a party have supported the principle of GATT on the several occasions when GATT has come before this house in its original form and in the form of later agreements based upon it, but we have not been able to close our eyes to the fact that in recent years, while the United States congress did vest in the administration the powers under which that administration signed the general agreement on tariffs and trade, nevertheless that congress turned around later and enacted legislation that violated not only the spirit of GATT but indeed its letter as well. I refer to the Andresen amendment of several years ago and the succeeding moves on the part of congress to erect barriers against the importation of Canadian dairy products.
We have seen a succession of attempts to raise tariffs and apply quotas and restrictions on the import of Canadian grains into the United States, recent attempts to apply tariffs upon the importation of fish sticks, hardboard and other Canadian products. No one can view the extent to which Canada is being drawn into the trading and economic orbit of the United States without very serious misgivings and a feeling of insecurity. To top it all, we see the United States proceeding to dispose of its farm surplus by putting $2 billion at the disposal of the administration in order that exports of agricultural produce by the United States may be subsidized, creating thereby very unfair competition for the Canadian farmer to face.
Let me just say this in conclusion on this particular subject. We as a party in Her Majesty's loyal opposition have supported GATT. Canada has lived up to her obligations under GATT; but we call upon the United States to do as much. We are not unmindful of the fact that eight years ago the GATT


signatories agreed that they would simplify customs procedures. Canada fulfilled her obligations in that respect. However, after eight years much remains to be done by the United States to fulfil her obligations in that regard. We have seen instead quantitative restrictions and other devices, the use of escape clauses and other provisions that GATT contains, to obtain for that country benefits that other signatories to GATT have not obtained for themselves.

This policy of national development is one born of the invincible confidence of the Conservative party in Canada's future. We are optimists for Canada, but we are realists as well. This great patrimony that a beneficent providence has given to this country is in our hands now. We can be worthy or unworthy custodians of it.
Canada holds a high position in the world, and that position is going to become of increasing importance. With it come increasing obligations, and to discharge those increasing obligations Canada needs to be strong. If Canada is strong, strengthened by the kind of policy we are advocating here today in this amendment, we shall at the same time strengthen this continent, the commonwealth, the free world and the entire cause of freedom. Sir, we are not dogmatic on this subject. We have never said Canada can be selfsufficient, but we say there is a great opportunity here for the application of this policy of national development. I wish to quote this extract from the speech by Mr. Gibson:
Much as we would at times like to invoke it, British influence on the economic side of our national life is not very great. Thus to maintain a degree of economic independence we have to develop our own economic policies.
This implies that we have economic objectives which can command agreement across our rather diverse country. In my opinion, the fundamental objective on which there seems to be the widest agreement is not economic at all-it is that we in Canada wish to remain an individual and developing national entity and not to become a part or a mere satellite of the United States. If we accept this fundamental conclusion, which I can think most Canadians would, certain economic conclusions appear to follow. The primary one is that the Canadian economy should be an economic reality and not merely a series of tributary areas whose orientation is largely toward adjoining parts of the United States. Political independence in any real sense needs a material basis and would scarcely be practicable in a divided and dependent economy. If Canada is to remain an economic reality, it further follows, as it always has in the past, that Canada must have a national policy of developing east-west communications across her country and east-west lines of trade.
We do not advocate waving any big stick at our friends in the United States, but we do assert that it is not the destiny of Canada to be the trade satellite or the dumping ground of any country in all the world. We think much can be done to shake our United States neighbours out of their complacent attitude toward Canada and toward Canada's economic interests.
The Canadian people are the greatest resource of this country. We wish, sir, to be good neighbours, staunch allies, helpful

Our choice in practice is rather between having some national economic policies of our own and becoming a divided and ineffectual satellite of the United States.
Then further he says:
If we wish to retain and strengthen our national identity we must develop more cohesion in our economic life and objectives.
This policy we advocate will help Canada develop that cohesion in our economic life and objectives which is needed. So I say, sir, that the destiny of Canada as a good neighbour, as a staunch ally, as a helpful friend, as the unwavering supporter of the free way of life, will best be served by the policy of national development which was set forth in the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition.

As I listened to the want of confidence motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition it seemed to me he must be speaking of some country other than Canada, although he did mention Canada. What did he say? He said the welfare of the Canadian people requires the adoption now of a national development policy which will develop our national resources for the maximum benefit of all parts of Canada.
May I call his attention to the fact that we started that policy on an exceedingly active scale back in 1940. The progress from 1940 to 1945 was stimulated by the urgency of producing weapons of war. However, let me point out that after 1945 there was no pause in that policy. No country has ever witnessed the national development, the development of our national resources and the increase in processing of those resources in this country to the extent that the people of Canada have witnessed it during the past decade and a half.
We speak of the present unfavourable trade balance; fostering wider participation by Canadians in the development of their resources and promoting greater opportunities of employment for a steadily increasing population. I am going to discuss those matters as we proceed, but I can say that all those things are being attended to and have been attended to over a very considerable period.
First, as the result of a balanced economic growth, financed largely by Canadian savings but assisted materially in certain key industries by foreign capital, know-how and enterprise, Canadians have enjoyed the benefit of prosperity unparalleled in the history of the country. Jobs are more plentiful; incomes are
9, 1956
Natural Resources-Development higher and so are living standards. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the economic policies pursued by the Canadian government, designed to encourage the development of our national resources and our secondary industries, have been sound and eminently successful.
I am sorry that I did not have the advantage of members of the official opposition in knowing what we would be discussing today and therefore I am meeting a prepared speech with a speech I have attempted to put together with scissors, largely from speeches I have made over a period outside this house.
I shall first discuss the trade situation. It is not surprising that this remarkable record of expansion and rising standards of living should be accompanied by equally remarkable levels of foreign trade. Indeed, it is not too much to say that the present economic activity could not be sustained without record exports and record imports. A high level of export demand is essential to the economic health of the Canadian economy. Rising exports have, in fact, been one of the main reasons for the rapid recovery from the mild recession of 1954. On the other hand, larger imports have been equally essential to meet the rising demands of Canadians for consumer and capital goods. The greater the prosperity, the more rapid the expansion, the higher the level of imports. Exports rose by 10 per cent in 1955 above the previous year. In the first five months of this year the increase over 1955 was 12 per cent, and in January, February and May the increase was between 17 per cent and 18 per cent over the same months of 1955.
We are undoubtedly on our way to a new record for exports, both in volume and value, well beyond anything that a year or two ago would have seemed attainable in 1956. As hon. members are aware, wheat exports have contributed substantially to this remarkable showing. After a slow start last fall, demand began to pick up about October or November. Then followed a period of sustained buying unique in my experience as minister of this department. Within the last few months we have seen wheat moving out of all our ports in steady and large volume. Exports of wheat and flour will probably reach, and perhaps exceed, 300 million bushels during the crop year 1955-56, an increase of 50 million bushels over the previous year when exports were at about average or normal levels.
As far as our other main exports are concerned, with a few exceptions we are exporting about as much as is available for export. In most important areas the limiting factor is supply, not demand, a fact which
5796	HOUSE OF
Natural Resources-Development is responsible for many of the larger expansion projects now under way in Canada. Further increases in exports can therefore be expected to follow upon completion of new capacity for the production and distribution of such items as aluminum, copper, iron ore, petroleum, uranium, pulp and paper and various types of chemicals. Canada is particularly fortunate to be an efficient supplier of those raw and processed materials so much in demand in the neighbouring United States and throughout the world.
There are exceptions, of course, even in a year of such phenomenal over-all results. Exports of lumber, for example, are now running a little below last year's unusually high sales, mainly as a result of the drawing down of defence stocks in the United Kingdom; but, by and large, our export trade is flourishing.
As hon. members are well aware from the comprehensive reports issued by the bureau
of statistics, there have been even greater increases in imports. In the current year, to date, imports have been nearly one-third higher than in the same period last year. As I said at the outset of these remarks, these extraordinary imports reflect the extraordinary levels of economic activity now prevailing in Canada. In particular they reflect the unusually rapid pace of development now under way.
Twice a year my department makes a survey of investment intentions of private industry and governments. At the beginning of 1956 this survey indicated a 21 per cent increase in capital expenditures to the highest levels on record. The department is just about to publish its mid-year survey. To my astonishment this survey indicates an upward revision in 1956 plans which now involve outlays 28 per cent above actual outlays in 1955. A major upsurge in imports would seem to be the natural consequence of such a situation. Many of the goods normally produced in Canada are simply not available in sufficient quantities to meet the present level of requirements.
For example, even though Canadian steel mills have been operating at capacity since early in 1955, imports of rolling mill products in recent months have been running at about double the rate of a year ago. As for cement, more than the normal volume of supplies from abroad will be needed this season notwithstanding greatly increased domestic capacity. Apart from this increase in over-all size, the changing composition of this year's investment program is also contributing to larger import totals. Most of the increase in capital outlays this year is for industrial expansion involving extensive purchases of machinery


and equipment, much of which can be obtained only from foreign sources.
In consumer goods, some of the sharpest increases are to be found in new types of goods not yet available in quantity from Canadian plants. It is apparent, therefore, that a very large proportion of the increased volume of goods coming into Canada has been necessary to supplement domestic supplies. While imports of goods which compete directly with Canadian products have also increased, this increase has not prevented higher production levels in the domestic industries concerned.
With very few exceptions activity in Canada's secondary manufacturing industries is now running well ahead of the levels prevailing in 1954. These considerations suggest that in the circumstances now prevailing in Canada a rapid rise in imports is not to be deplored. On the contrary, it is highly desirable. In the first place, it helps to speed industrial expansion while market opportunities are still present. Second, it helps to ease the pressure on domestic resources and thereby prevents inflationary tendencies and unhealthy speculative excesses which might benefit individual groups but would react to the disadvantage of the community at large. Even those who are prone to deplore the rising level of imports would, I am sure, be concerned if a prolonged steel strike in the United States were to bring about a reduction of imports at the expense of those great projects which depend upon the availability of structural and other types of steel produced in United States mills.
A much sharper rise in imports than of exports has resulted in a substantially increased deficit in merchandise trade. It is customary for Canada to run a deficit on nonmerchandise transactions, and when this is added to the imbalance on trade the resulting deficit on all current account transactions amounted to $345 million for the first quarter of 1956. In other words, Canada's international balance of payments on current transactions is at the moment showing a deficit amounting to about one-quarter of total receipts from abroad.
Balance of payment deficits sometimes occur when countries, in one way or another, attempt to maintain living standards out of line with their productive potentialities. For this reason adverse international balances are often associated in the public mind with financial weakness. In fact, for most countries a current deficit of the same relative magnitude as that now being encountered by Canada would mean serious trouble.

In Canada's present circumstances, however, this deficit is not a reflection of weakness but of strength; it is the direct result of rapid industrial growth and rising living standards which are no more than commensurate with the nation's productive capacities. In fact, as I have indicated, a major portion of current investment is for additions to capacity in export industries. In other words, the very strength of Canada's export prospects is one of the principal reasons for the current import surplus.
Present expansion plans also involve substantial additions for the production of goods now being purchased from abroad. Both these types of expansion will primarily affect trade with the United States. Further increases in the production of forest products, minerals and chemicals will tend to boost our future exports to that country. At the same time the round of expansion now taking place in steel, fuels and various chemicals will replace goods now being purchased from United States suppliers. It is important that the present deficit with the United States be considered in the light of these underlying developments.
The most conclusive evidence of the basic strength of Canada's external position is the fact that despite the large deficit on current account, we are not encountering balance of payment difficulties. The increasing rate at which investment funds are coming into the country giver ample proof of the confidence placed in Canada's position and future prospects. So far this inflow of funds has been sufficient to match the rising deficit on current account, with but an inconsequential decline in official holdings of gold and United States dollars and with continuing firmness in the external value of the Canadian dollar The Canadian dollar is stronger now than it was for some time in spite of the large trade deficit.
There might be some reason for concern about the present situation if foreign investors were shying away from Canada, if they were worried about Canadian economic or political stability. There might be some reason for concern about the present situation if we were living beyond our means or were building up uneconomic industries. But this is not the situation. Foreign investors all over the world have confidence in Canada. They are confident that this country will continue to be in a position to meet its obligations. They are strengthened in that belief by the evidence that a great deal of the new investment is going into industries which help to increase exports or reduce imports, thus adding to Canadian financial and economic stability for future years.
Natural Resources-Development I am astonished when I listen to criticism oi the current trade deficit, which is so essential to our current phase of expansion and development. Perhaps, however, the opposition is really opposed to the development of the country but hesitates to say so, since this point of view would not be popular with the people of Canada. Certainly they would find themselves unpopular with the provincial governments of this country which, without exception, are promoting the development of their respective territories and are encouraging industries from outside the country to establish in Canada.

I would now like to say something about the processing of raw materials. Most of the complaints we hear about the lack of processing of domestic raw materials in Canada are based on two premises: (1) that by using more of these materials at home we would be providing more jobs for Canadians, and (2) that if we cannot use these resources at home or cannot sell them abroad in processed or fabricated form, we should let them remain in the ground, the forest or the sea, to protect the national heritage of future generations of Canadians.
Let me say right from the start that the Canadian government is just as much interested as the members on the opposite side in seeing that a high level of employment is maintained in our country, and that the national interest is safeguarded for the benefit of the present as well as future generations of Canadians. In fact many of the Canadian government's economic policies are directed to this very end; and I submit, Mr. Speaker, they have been eminently successful, as the post-war record of economic achievement in Canada shows very clearly.
The main point to remember is that in many fields if it were not for our export markets, Canadian production would have to be cut back severely and costs of production would rise materially. In wheat, for example in a good crop year we export up to two thirds of our output. In nickel we export some 99 per cent of our production, in asbestos 96 per cent, in newsprint 93 per cent, in aluminum 87 per cent, and in copper 66 per cent. As to iron ore, we exported last year about 84 per cent of our total domestic production, and this proportion may rise further over the next few years as production is likely to expand at a considerably more rapid rate than domestic consumption.
The point has been made that by keeping raw materials at home, processing them here and then fabricating finished products,

Natural Resources-Development employment will be increased in Canada. Well, I submit, Mr. Speaker, it we were to stop exports of a number of our important industrial materials the opposite would happen. We would have less employment, incomes would fall, and the standard of living of Canadians would drop. Obviously we cannot use some 100 times as much nickel as we are in fact doing, nor 25 times as much asbestos, 14 times as much newsprint, 7J- times as much aluminum, six times as much iron ore, and three times as much copper, as we would have to in order to make use of all these raw materials we are producing. Nor can we eat three times as much bread and cake, which we would have to do to use up all our wheat at home.
Two things could happen if we stopped exports of this or that important raw material: (1) our customers could turn to alternative sources of supply. Don't let us fool ourselves. There are plenty of natural resources available in the world. They may not be as conveniently located as they are in Canada, or they may be in countries with a less stable economic climate and government than we have here in Canada. But if our customers abroad could not get the raw materials and foodstuffs they urgently need and in the form they wanted them from us, I am sure they would develop sources of supply somewhere else, or they might turn to alternative materials that in the end might serve their purposes just as well. (2) Since we could not possibly use all the materials at home, we would have to close some of our mines, mills and factories. People laid off in these industries would spend less, affecting people employed in our fabricating industries and in our service industries. Unemployment would spread and the country would be going down instead of up.
I hardly think even the members on the opposite side of this house would want to see this happen in Canada. But this is what could happen and in my considered opinion would happen if Canadians resorted to artificial measures on a broad scale to interfere with the forces of the market, and in the process disturbed the balanced economic growth which Canada has been undergoing in the more recent period. In the present buoyant state of the Canadian economy the argument that keeping raw materials in this country increases jobs is not only academic, it is also fallacious.
One of the most noteworthy developments in Canada is the high degree of industrialization of our economy. Every fourth person working in our country is now employed in manufacturing industries, and approximately one out of every three dollars of our national


income is earned in Canadian industrial plants. No wonder, then, that Canada has become an important importer of industrial raw materials and fuel, including bauxite, cotton, wool, coal and crude oil. Last year, for example, we imported $530 million of industrial materials in raw form. We exported a total of $3-25 billion of industrial materials. But of this amount $2-8 billion represented materials sold abroad in processed form. Only about $425 million went out in raw form. Hence in our trade in raw materials and fuels used by industry, Canada was a net importer of industrial raw materials, to the tune of some $105 million in 1955.
This situation, of course, is not static. We are likely to export more iron ore in the future. But then some of our other industrial materials which are now exported in raw form may be moving into the category of materials processed at home in some form or another; for example, pulpwood, copper, etc. It is well to remember when we complain about exports of our raw materials that we import raw materials to the value of $105 million in excess of the value of the raw materials that we export.
I have heard the question asked, why are we exporting so much iron ore? Why are we not using more at home? Well, hon. members will be interested to hear that out of 5-1 million tons of iron ore used last year by Canada's five largest steel mills, 3-8 million tons were imported. In the midst of Canada's greatest surpluses of iron ore, our steel manufacturers are presently using almost three times as much imported ore as domestic ore.
There are good reasons for this. Steel makers need different types of iron ore for mixing purposes. Some types are not available in Canada or only at much higher prices than they can buy these types of ores, say, in the United States. Why should a Canadian steel company pay higher prices for Canadian iron ore if it can get that iron ore at a lower price somewhere else? Would opposition members recommend that Canadian steel companies be forced to pay more for Canadian ore and thus price themselves out of the market? Does it not make more economic sense to buy the iron ore in the cheapest market to enable the Canadian steel industry to remain competitive? Or in a broader national context, does it not make economic sense for Canada to sell iron ore, crude oil or any other industrial raw material to the United States where this can be done competitively, and to bring in the same or similar materials from the United States where these materials can be bought more

cheaply than Canadian products, which because of added transportation costs might be higher priced?
Incidentally, one of our largest Canadian steel companies has substantial sums of money invested in United States iron ore mines. If Canada stopped the export of iron ore to the United States or made it difficult for such ore to get to the United States, could Canadian importers of iron ore rightly expect any different treatment? May I remind the house that Canada depends quite heavily on imports of industrial materials in both the raw and processed forms from the United States. It is not just iron ore; we also buy from the United States oil, coal, cotton, sulphur, brimstone, phosphate rock, etc.
The United States has traditionally protected Canada's supply of raw materials in times of shortage, and the Canadian government appreciates the co-operative attitude of the United States administration. You will recall how our friends to the south continued to supply Canada with such scarce items as steel during world war II and during the period of rearmament which followed the outbreak of war in Korea, even though that meant cutting down the domestic consumption. Canada did the same with such materials as nickel, copper, aluminum, etc. North America has a good deal to gain from the efficient development of these resources and from a continuously expanding exchange of such materials. Our hope, of course, is that more and more of the materials we supply as our part of the exchange will be processed at home. We have made a good deal of progress in this direction, as I shall elaborate later, and we believe we will continue to make good progress.
The Leader of the Opposition says we are not processing enough of our raw materials in Canada. What does he mean by enough? I have already pointed out that it just does not make economic sense to smelt in Canada every ton of iron ore we are capable of producing, or to refine every barrel of oil that comes out of the ground. If we look at the actual achievements in the growth of our processing industries they are remarkable indeed, and are perhaps the best answer to those who want to give the impression that our processing industries are shrinking violets and are making little progress.
Increased processing of raw materials in Canada is reflected in substantial expansion in the production of a number of our major industries in the post-war period. For example, the value of manufactures of primary iron and steel rose three times over the last decade, reaching a total of half a billion dollars last

The chemical industry is perhaps an outstanding example of the rapid industrial progress and diversification the Canadian economy has been experiencing in the more recent period. After the war's end much of these gains were consolidated, with new chemicals being produced in Canada as accessibility of raw materials and the growth of domestic and foreign markets warranted.
A large number of chemicals have been produced for the first time in Canada since the end of the war, or have been produced by means of new and more efficient processes. There are too many hard words in that paragraph.

On the contrary, our processing and advanced manufacturing industries are expanding rapidly. This expansion is well balanced and is accompanied by growth in our resources industries which cater to both Canadian and foreign markets.
As a result of Canada's rapid process of industrialization our country now occupies a position second only to the United States in terms of output per capita of manufacturing industries. 1 am sure hon. members will be gratified to hear that in relation to our total

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would now like to put before the house a few key facts about foreign investment in Canada and Canadian investment abroad. I propose to show:

Second, that in relation to our growing productive capacity the burden of foreign investment is declining, while Canadian investment abroad is increasing by leaps and bounds.
Third, that Canadian ownership of capital employed in Canadian industry has increased more rapidly than non-residential ownership. The trend in over-all terms is toward the Canadianization of Canadian industry.
I shall conclude with a few observations about the benefits accruing to the Canadian economy from the inflow of foreign capital into Canadian resources and industrial development, and I shall mention some of the difficulties that are being encountered.
The free and unhampered flow of foreign investment into Canada has brought so many benefits to this country that it certainly is entitled to a fair and unbiased hearing from the Canadian people. We do not want such discussion to be carried out in an atmosphere of emotionalism and ignorance, but rather in one in which common sense and good will prevail. I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that after considering the facts Canadians will continue to endorse the policies of this government.

I listened patiently this afternoon to some of the greatest rot I have heard in my life, so please listen to me this evening. Canada has always been dependent on a substantial inflow of capital to develop the country, to expand industry, to build a transportation network and to create the many other facilities which a rapidly expanding economy requires.
In the 89 years since confederation there has been an important change in the pattern of financing Canadian investment. In the nineteenth century the overwhelming proportion of our capital expansion was financed by capital coming from the United Kingdom and the United States. Then during the first two decades of this century the rapid settlement, urbanization and industrialization that took place made it possible for Canadians to accumulate a more significant volume of savings, which found its way into Canadian investment. While statistics of this type are scarce, what information we have suggests tha'. something like two-thirds of Canadian investment was financed by funds from abroad during this period. The years that followed saw a further improvement, and by the late 192U S about one-half of gross capital formation in Canada was financed from Canadian savings, the other half through non-resident financing.
During world war II Canada herself was able to finance almost wholly the capital

expenditures on facilities required to turn out munitions of war, to train the armed forces, and to keep the civilian economy going. After the war's end foreign investors started sending capital to Canada again to participate in our economic expansion. Still about 80 per cent of all of Canada's gross capital formation was financed from Canadian savings and 20 per cent through direct foreign financing in the period 1946 to 1949. In the last five years the inflow of foreign capital has been stepped up, and the ratio of Canadian to foreign financing of gross capital formation has been about three to one.
In fact, nowever, Canadian savings available for investment were much greater than these figures would suggest. A good portion of these savings were invested abroad. From 1946 to 1949 and for some years before that, and again in 1952, Canada was a net exporter of capital. So if one allows for Canadian investments abroad and the use of foreign resources as a percentage of net capital formation, it turns out that not more than 6 per cent of Canadian investment in the post-war period depended on foreign resources.
To look at foreign investment in Canada in its proper perspective, we must see it in the light of what Canadians are doing abroad. I have noticed that some hon. members on the opposite side have been quoting from a recent publication of the dominion bureau of statistics, "Canada's International Investment Position 1926-1954". I have noticed how careful they have been in not bringing to light any facts or figures which would bring out the positive achievements of Canadians in this field of foreign investment. The reasons are fairly clear, since most of the trends are favourable to the Canadian position. Instead of being proud of that, opposition members prefer to pick on a few figures, and out of context at that, to support their claim that Canadian industry is going to the dogs because of foreign domination.

By the end of 1955 gross liabilities to other countries had risen to $14-5 billion, amounting to about double what they had been in 1939. Canada's gross external assets had risen to $7 billion, or about four times what they had been in 1939. Currently for every $2 Canadians owe abroad, $1 is due

Natural Resources-Development them. If this trend continues I would not be surprised to see Canada in the next quarter of a century move from a position of a debtor to that of a creditor nation. In fact, as I said earlier, in some years we already have been making available to other countries more capital than we have been bringing in. In a way, then, one can say that for some years Canada has already been a creditor nation. But this trend is likely to become even more clearly apparent as our economy gathers strength and savings continue to accumulate in Canada at a rapid rate.
We hear little complaint about foreign investment in Canada other than that directed at investment by United States residents. Now, out of the $14-5 billion of money Canada owes to other countries, about $13-2 billion is foreign capital invested in Canada and the remainder is Canadian dollar holdings of non-residents and shortterm assets. Of the latter amount some three-quarters is United States investments.
More detailed figures available for 1954 enable us to compare the long-term investments of Canadians in the United States with those of United States residents in Canada. Hon. members will be interested to learn that at the end of 1954 the average Canadian had invested $121 in the United States, while the average United States investor had invested less than half that amount in Canada, $59. To suggest that the average Canadian investor is a timid soul, as I have heard it said, while the United States investor is bold and venturesome, is not quite supported by the facts, if we consider Canadian and United States investments in each other's countries on a per capita basis.
This is in no way intended to disparage the importance of the large United States stake in Canada, or the enterprise and imagination shown by some of the large United States companies in participating in Canadian resources and industrial development. But the point I would like to make is that for a country as small as Canada with only about one-tenth the population of the United States and one-fifteenth of its national output, Canadians have made substantial investments abroad. The bulk of it is in the United States, but fairly sizeable amounts are also invested in the United Kingdom and other commonwealth countries, Latin America, western Europe, Africa and Asia.
Now, to come to the role of foreign capital in Canada, let us consider for a moment what foundations there are for the scare stories which are being spread by some members of the opposition, which have led the hon. member for Broadview to use the picturesque phrase of Canada becoming an "economic

Natural Resources-Development vassal" of the United States, or the hon. member for Three Rivers to revive the ghost of economic colonialism, which I thought was buried 89 years ago.
Foreign investors have shown preferences for investment in certain sectors of the Canadian economy, particularly oil and natural gas, mining, and certain branches of manufacturing such as motor cars, appliances, electrical and electronic equipment. In these fields in which they have concentrated they have invested large amounts, and in some sectors they frequently own or control the bulk of the assets. But we have to see foreign investment in Canada in its proper perspective, and that is in relation to the growth of capital owned by Canadian residents. The fact of the matter is that Canadian capital has been expanding over the last decade and a half at a rate about twice as great as that of foreign capital in Canada. This is illustrated by the growth of resident-owned capital in selected Canadian industries from $7'4 billion in 1939 to $17-2 billion in 1953, an increase of 132 per cent. During the same period non-resident capital rose from $4 [DOT] 5 billion to $8 -3 billion, an increase of 84 per cent.
There is the further point that Canadian business has relied more and more on domestic sources for the capital needed for this expansion. As a result foreign direct investment in Canada has been expanding at a much slower pace than has outlay by private business. Over the period 1939 to 1955, for example, foreign direct investment in Canada more than tripled while outlay by private business increased to nine times the 1939 level.
I have heard it suggested that the growth of foreign investment in Canada is putting unbearable strain on the economy of the country. Those who make this suggestion want to give the impression that our foreign investors are interested in nothing but making a quick profit. The fact is that a large proportion of the Canadian earnings of foreign investors is reinvested in Canadian development. Further, Canada's economy has been growing at such a rapid rate that the role of foreign investment in relation to our productive capacity has diminished and will continue to do so.
You will recall that I mentioned that our gross liabilities to other countries have about doubled between 1939 and 1955. Over this same period our gross national product has risen to four times what it was before the war. Obviously as our productive capacity continues to grow more rapidly than the inflow of foreign capital, the burden of carrying this foreign investment is reduced.

The Prime Minister should not have said special measures "should perhaps be taken" to improve the economy of the Atlantic provinces; I think as prime minister of this country he should have said "special measures must be taken" to improve the economy of the Atlantic provinces. He went on to say:
This merits and is receiving attention from many of us. However, the initiative and the ideas, the energies and the determination to accomplish

this redevelopment cannot originate in other parts of Canada; they must come from the Atlantic area.
That was looked on as a challenge by the people of the maritime provinces and eastern Canada, and I might say the challenge has been accepted. It has certainly been accepted by the four premiers of the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. They are meeting today in the city of Fredericton, and I can assure the Prime Minister and this government they will come forward with plans and schemes-they will not be altogether new, because they have been recommended time and time again before dominion-provincial conferences-which if put into effect will greatly benefit these provinces in future.
I should like to quote briefly from some of the remarks our premier made at the dominion-provincial conference in 1955. When speaking of the processing of natural resources in my own province, Mr. Flemming said:
The government of New Brunswick will not stand idly by and allow these natural resources to lie dormant. Your government is determined that our mineral wealth shall not be dug up and carted away from this province to be processed elsewhere.
That should be the policy not only of the province of New Brunswick but as far as possible it should be the policy of the whole of the Dominion of Canada. He continued:
The aim of the government is to supply the mining companies with power cheap enough to insure the economic processing of our minerals in New Brunswick.
As I said, this same policy could very well be followed for the whole Dominion of Canada. I might also say it is the same policy which was followed by our leader when he was premier of the province of Ontario. It was practised in Ontario at that time, and I am satisfied it will be practised in the Dominion of Canada when the leader of the Conservative party becomes the prime minister of this country. At the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects Mr. Flemming, speaking of the industrial and economic growth of Canada, said:
As a matter of fact, for nearly one hundred years the relative economic level of this province_

Mr. Speaker, I listened most carefully this afternoon to that hour-long speech by the Leader of the Opposition. I think for 50 minutes of his speech I wondered how he could ever come down to any point of criticism of the government, because in that 50 minutes practically everything he said was at least by implication eulogistic of the government which was responsible for the very prosperous conditions in Canada to which he was referring Therefore 1 make it quite clear at the outset that I have certainly no quarrel to pick with at least nine-tenths of the speech made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition, nor for that matter with the speakers from other parties on that side.
However, I must say that I was a little surprised when the Leader of the Opposition got down to his actual motion of want of confidence in the government and itemized the particular reasons why he thought that motion should be adopted. As I see it the two most important points he made were first
